speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to give the house a statement on trade and financial arrangements between the governments of the United Kingdom and Canada, for which hon. members have been waiting.
As the house is aware, it was recently agreed with the United Kingdom government that a mission should come to Ottawa to discuss the trade and financial arrangements between the two countries, with special1 reference to the United Kingdom's purchasing program of Canadian supplies in 1948.
The mission, headed by Sir Percival Leisching, Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Food, arrived in Ottawa on the 25th November. There has since been held with them a series of most valuable and comprehensive discussions covering the whole field of our trade with the United Kingdom, and I am happy to announce that as a result of the exchanges which have taken place agreement has now been reached with the United Kingdom government on all matters under review.
Both countries at the present time face a common difficulty, namely, a shortage of United States dollars. From the Canadian standpoint, this and other factors limit the extent to which the balance of the credit, provided for under the Financial Agreement Act of 1946, can be drawn on in order to make supplies available to the United Kingdom. Canada has made a very great effort-not exceeded by that of any other state-to assist in the restoration and reconstruction of countries damaged and destroyed by war. But she cannot continue indefinitely to export on credit, and import for cash. From the United Kingdom standpoint, her own shortage of hard currency equally limits the extent to which she can afford at this time to make payment in dollars for goods supplied from Canada.
The discussions with the United Kingdom mission centred around (1) the necessity for Canada of maintaining a balanced agricultural program and (2) the basic dollar difficulty in both countries. However, though there may have been a shortage of dollars on both sides, there has been also on both sides a surplus of good will and mutual understanding. Also, if there has been a common difficulty, there has been a common objective, the maintenance at this time and the extension in the future of a stable and steady market in the United Kingdom for Canadian farm produce. This means a restored and vigorous economy in the United Kingdom and a steady rise in her industrial production and exports. It means also a prosperous Canadian agriculture, the value of which has become increasingly realized in the United Kingdom during the war and post-war years.
Canada wishes to continue to send to the United Kingdom all those supplies of foodstuffs and raw materials which are playing such a vital part in sustaining the United Kingdom's reconstruction program. The United Kingdom's need for such supplies, in order to maintain the progress now visible in her recovery, is so strong and compelling that any interruption at this time would have very serious consequences.
In the arrangement for the provision of supplies, however, Canada has not been asked and will not be asked to go further than her financial situation permits. Likewise the United Kingdom will itself decide how to dispose of its present limited financial resources in the way most effective for its recovery.
It is in this spirit of mutual interest, mutual understanding and mutual assistance that the discussions have been conducted. It is in the same spirit that agreement has been reached.
The agreed arrangement provides for the continuance of the wheat agreement with the United Kingdom and for the continuance and renewal of the contracts for livestock products at prices adjusted accordingly. Thus the balance of Canadian agricultural production will be preserved, and there will be no interruption in these supplies to the British market.
The arrangement also provides for continued supplies to the United Kingdom of certain raw materials needed for reconstruction purposes, in particular timber and non-
Trade Agreements

ferrous metals, though the quantities have been adjusted in relation both to United Kingdom needs and the demands for these products from other countries.
In estimating the probable trading deficit on this basis, account has been taken of the increased exports from the United Kingdom and the sterling area which, following these discussions, are expected to be made available for the Canadian market during the coming year. The arrangement provides that in the three months period up to the 31st March next, the expected deficit of 145 million dollars should be financed by drawings on the Canadian credit up to 45 million dollars and by the payment by the United Kingdom of 100 million dollars. Our government will review the position at the end of the three months period.
A statement substantially similar to this is being made today in London by the United Kingdom Prime Minister.

He stated in one place that there had been agreement in all matters under review. Might I ask him to tell the house whether there has been agreement on the amounts to be provided and on the prices to be paid under the various contracts we already have with Britain?
And I have one other question. The announcement just made relates to the matter to be discussed this afternoon in the resolution dealing with the extension for three months of the Agricultural Products Act. Up to the present we have not had notice of any changed position by the government. Now the Prime Minister makes a statement announcing some changes, the implications of which we cannot readily grasp. My suggestion to the government is this. In view of the changed position of the government with respect to certain of these matters, and in view of the debate that is now on or which will begin in just a few minutes, I suggest the propriety of delaying this debate for two or three hours until the members of the house can examine the statement the Prime Minister has made, and that we proceed with the debate in which we were engaged yesterday or some other one. If the Prime Minister could indicate whether there has been any agreement on prices in

these contracts and the amounts to be supplied, could we have that information at this time?
One other sentence in the Prime Minister's statement is confusing. He said the wheat agreement was to be continued very much as it is, as I gathered, but with respect to livestock matters he said prices were to be accordingly adjusted. To me that sentence meant nothing. Perhaps it could be explained or enlarged upon either by the Prime Minister or the Minister of Agriculture.

speechtext:
Probably this is as good a
time as any to answer both questions, the one asked first by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) and repeated now in different form by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank).
The suggestion was made a few minutes ago that something should be said with regard to quantity and price which would permit of discussion of this question when we come to the resolution. I would say that the paragraph in the announcement just made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) dealing with quantity reads in this way:
Canada wishes to continue to send to the United Kingdom all those supplies of foodstuffs and raw materials which are playing such a vital part in sustaining the United Kingdom's reconstruction program.
That states Canada's position in regard to the quantity. Then it continues.:
The United Kingdom's need for such supplies, in order to maintain the progress now visible in her recovery, is so strong and compelling that any interruption at this time would have very serious consequences.
The interpretation, I believe, that the house will be justified in placing upon those words is that, so far as foodstuffs are concerned, Canada is anxious to deliver to Great Britain her surplus of foodstuffs in question. The figures with regard to wheat are now known, of course.
With respect to the surplus of other foodstuffs in question, I believe I should repeat something that was said at the last session, namely that up until now we have been using contracts, not only for the purpose of supplying to Great Britain what she expects to get from this country but for the purpose of inducing farmers to increase production in certains directions. It has been decided to depart from that policy and to estimate the amount of foodstuffs which we believe can be supplied during the year ahead and to write that figure into the contract. Therefore any figure which is put into the contract will not be a reduced figure asked for by Great Britain or a reduced figure insisted upon by Canada; it will result from the determination as nearly as possible of the exact amount of food which we can supply under the contract. That will

be the quantity which will then be placed in the contract and will be intended to cover our surplus.
The other question was with regard to price. The paragraph dealing with that reads as follows:
The agreed atrangement provides for the continuance of the wheat agreement with the United Kingdom-
I think all members will agree that in so far as price in relation to wheat is concerned, that is set out in the contract. We know the terms that apply to it. Then the report continues:

and for the continuance and renewal of the contracts for livestock products at prices adjusted accordingly. Thus the balance of Canadian agricultural production will be preserved, and there will be no interruption in these supplies to the British market.
There is one thing I should like to point out with regard to the matter of price. Agreement in principle was reached within the last few hours, or at the latest one might say yesterday. It will be understood that it would be impossible for officials, some of whom are in London and some of whom are on this side, to come to' an agreement within the few hours that have intervened as to the exact price. It would be difficult for me to say at.this moment exactly what the price will be, and it might be difficult to say that even before tomorrow night. But the principle which is to underlie the setting of the price has been agreed upon and it is stated in the sentence which I have just read.
Feed grain prices have a relationship to the wheat price and the increase to the present feed grain prices have had an effect upon the cost of producing other commodities. These are facts which will have to be taken into consideration in setting a new price for food products upon which the agreement is to be made. Those food products are bacon, beef, cheese and eggs. The contracts will carry throughout the year and there are certain understandings with regard to matters in the future.

be difficult to be more specific at the moment than I have been in connection with this matter, even if I had more information. I believe it is essential that as soon as possible after the exact price which is to apply in the contract is known, those prices should come into effect. If one were to announce that there are to be higher prices for a certain commodity on January 1 there might be great difficulty in getting sufficient supplies on our own markets in the intervening period in order to take care of our own requirements. I think it will be necessary to have the discussions completed with Great Britain with regard to the exact price, and then when the prices are announced action should be taken immediately on our own markets and elsewhere. For that reason I suggest again that it may be impossible to give an exact figure before tomorrow night, but I think most hon. members who are interested in this question will have clearly in their own minds a figure which is fairly close to the one which will be in the contract.

speechtext: Mr. F. E. JAENICKE (Kindersley) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 5, to amend the Supreme Court Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the 13th January, 1947, the judicial committee of the privy council decided that the dominion parliament may, in the exercise of the wide amplitude of power conferred by section 101 of the British North America Act, vest the Supreme Court of Canada with final and exclusive civil and appellate jurisdiction within and for Canada and may accordingly deny any appeal to His Majesty in Council either from the supreme court or from any provincial court and regardless of whether the matter in question is within the exclusive legislative authority of the dominion or the provincial legislatures. The purpose of the present bill is to give effect to this decision of the privy council. It is exactly the same as the bill I introduced in this house last session.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext: Mr. STANLEY KNOWLES (Winnipeg North Centre) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 6, to amend the Railway Act.

subtopic: PENSION RIGHTS-BREAKS IN SERVICE FROM CERTAIN CAUSES
speechtext:
Section 122(1) (c) of the Railway Act gives to railway boards of directors authority to establish retirement or pension plans. This bill would add to the appropriate paragraph the following words:
Provided that in the administration of any railway retirement or pension plan, leave of

absence, suspension, dismissal followed by reinstatement, a temporary lay-off on account of reduction of staff, or absence due to an industrial dispute, strike or lock-out, shall not disqualify any railway employee from any retirement or pension rights or benefits to which he would otherwise be entitled.
The purpose of this amendment, which is exactly the same as Bill No. 24 of last session, is to make it perfectly clear that the pension rights of railway employees, provided such other conditions as are laid down in railway pensions plans are met, cannot be lost or abrogated because of a break in service for any of the reasons indicated in the proviso I have just read.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

1.	Under the Canadian Wheat Board Act, as amended in 1917, the Winnipeg grain exchange has no specific function in regard to the marketing of wheat. The house resumed, from Monday, December 15, consideration of the motion of Mr. Usley:
That, whereas section eleven of the Agricultural Products Act, being chapter ten of the statutes of 1947, provides that subject as thereinafter provided, that act shall expire on the thirty-first day of December, one thousand nine hundred and forty-seven, if parliament meets during November or December one thousand nine hundred and forty-seven, but if parliament does not so meet it shall expire on the sixtieth day after parliament first meets during the year one thousand nine hundred and forty-eight or on the thirty-first day of March, one thousand nine hundred and forty-eight, whichever date is the earlier: Provided that, if at any time while that act is in force, addresses are presented to the Governor General by the Senate and House of Commons respectively, praying that that act should be continued in force for a further period, not in any case exceeding one year, from the time at which it would otherwise expire and the governor in council so orders, that act shall continue in force for that further period.
And whereas it is considered desirable to continue the said act in force until the thirty-first day of March, one thousand nine hundred and forty-eight;
The following address he presented to His Excellency the Governor General of Canada:
To His Excellency Field Marshal The (Right Honourable Viscount Alexander of Tunis, Knight of the Most Noble Order of the Garter, Knight Grand Cross of the Most Honourable Order of the Bath, Knight Grand Cross of the Most Distinguished Order of Saint Michael and Saint George, Companion of the Most Exalted Order of the Star of India, Companion of the Distinguished Service Order, upon whom has been conferred the Decoration of the Military Cross, one of His Majesty's Aides-de-Camp General, Governor General and Commander-in-Chief of the Dominion of Canada.
May it Please Your Excellency:

Mr. Speaker, this resolution asks for an extension of the Agricultural Products Act until March 31, 1948. At the beginning let me say that I am agreeable to giving the minister this power; in fact, I do not know what good three months is going to do him because it

has just been intimated that the arrangements with Britain, are being extended and this power will certainly be needed to enable the minister to carry on.
Perhaps my greatest criticism of this measure is that the minister has not used the power which the act gave him. He could have gone much farther and given much more protection to the farmer in the buying of the different products which this measure covers. For years the farmer has been trying to catch up with people in other walks of life who have some established basis for the prices they receive for their labour and the things they have to sell. The farmer feels that the laws of supply and demand just do not work any more so far as the things he has to buy are concerned. He knows that the first charge against the things he has to. buy is the cost of producing them, and he is asking that the same law apply to the things he has to sell.
I spoke on milk production the other night. I am quite willing to admit that there is room for considerable improvement so far as feeding and breeding is concerned, but it should be remembered that if a cow gives more milk she has to be provided with more and: better feed, which has to be charged against the extra milk produced.
Farm labour is demanding decent wages and better conditions; and, since labour constitutes thirty per cent of the cost of producing milk, this will offset to a considerable extent any saving by better feeding and breeding. I think too little attention is being paid to lowering the cost of milk distribution. We are being led to believe that the dairy industry revolves around the business of buying and selling milk and dairy products, but that the producer and the consumer are of minor concern. I believe both consumer and producer would benefit by one of them going into the business of distributing milk at cost on a co-operative basis. Milk should pass from the producer to the consumer at the lowest possible price. It is in that direction that we should look when we think of lowering the price of milk to the consumer.
I want to ask the minister a question about eggs. The hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) brought that up a few minutes ago. The price has been forty-three cents a dozen for grade A, and for grade B it has been twenty-nine cents. Can the minister explain to the house why there is such a variation? We know that in country points in Manitoba where we have been shipping our eggs, when we get more B's than A's we say, ''We will sell the A's and take the B's home", and then there is an immediate improvement.

Agricultural Products Act
That is something the minister should look into because the farmer is being victimized to the extent of that variation of twelve cents. We the producers know that we do not produce B eggs but A. There may be some that are off-shaped, but those are kept at home. The price can be forty-three cents in the country, as was stated in the newspaper, and that means forty-one cents to the producer, if he takes them to the egg grading station.
I have here a cutting from the Ottawa Journal of a couple of nights ago. I quote:
Domestic egg prices are due for a sharp drop early in the new year, following a cut by about eight cents a dozen in the level paid producers by the government's special products board, the Journal today was informed.
Board prices for eggs on overseas contracts always have served as a floor level on the domestic market.
When the minister is answering the questions that have been put to him I want to know why, when we ship about twenty or twenty-five per cent of any agricultural product in the country, that should set the price for domestic supplies. Continuing, the Journal says:
To cushion the price cut for producers, the board may subsidize feed used by poultry farmers.
In recent weeks domestic prices of eggs have slipped from a late November peak which took grade A as high as 68 cents per dozen.
I think that is the retail price.
This premium grade today was bringing 57 cents, and pullet eggs were worth 48 cents per dozen.
While the board's producer prices will be cut by eight cents, the reduction to consumers will be on a smaller scale, but still appreciable.
I should like the minister to explain that because, if the farmer loses eight cents a dozen, why does the consumer not get the same reduction? I think the poultryman has had a raw deal. I am sure many people will support me in that statement because the price of his feed is going up and no one can get in and out in this business over-night. You have to plan ahead, and I do not need to tell the minister that taking the subsidy off coarse grains and allowing the grains to go on the open speculative market has added to the confusion of the poultryman.
In the production of eggs we use a lot of tankage. Before the packing house strike we could buy tankage for $2.95 in Winnipeg. Today we are paying $6.65. There is no reason for that, because tankage is only a by-product from the slaughter house. There is no justification whatever for it. Why should there be that discrepancy between $2.95 and $6.65? As
a matter of fact, I can give the minister data to show that at some places they are asking $7.05 for the same quantity of tankage.
The price the poultryman gets for eggs today, if he has a high producing flock, will allow him to break even, but if the flock goes to sixty-five and seventy per cent he will be ifl the red and will dispose of that flock, and I do not know if that is a very profitable thing to do either. I have here a statement showing that one poultryman became a little disgusted with the returns he was getting from his eggs-I can vouch that his flock consisted of year old hens-and he sent those hens back to the packing company, sixty-five of them. They averaged five and a quarter pounds each and the packing company paid him twelve cents a pound.
What did they grade?
Those birds graded A.
Which birds? On the other side?
Oh, no; they would never grade A.
They would be discarded.	.

I want to assure hon. members that this is a very serious matter because it is going to disrupt our agriculture economy as never before. People will not keep on producing if they are to get a raw deal like that. Now just follow that chicken through-
It wouldn't be the first chicken they followed.

No, some of these fellows have followed chickens before, but we shall leave that for the time being. When these fowl reached Winnipeg, or the next town where there was a poultry plant, they were worth twenty cents a pound. Today boiling fowl are selling at thirty-four and thirty-six cents a pound.
That is unfair. You can never have successful farming or have men remain in the sphere of agriculture if you treat them like that, I do not need to labour the point. The farmer gets twelve cents; the jobber, twenty cents; and the man who retails them gets thirty-four and thirty-six cents. I wonder if it can be that the packing company keeps filling its coolers until the time comes for a killing. There is someone making money and it is not the farmer. I can assure the minister- he is smiling-that his meat board has the power to check this sort of thing if he will make them get after these people.
I do not want to cover the whole agricultural economy. I simply wish to bring out one or two things that have been brought to
Agricultural Products Act

my attention as the representative of a farming community. I was in the northern part of my constituency before I came here, and I cannot speak to the house in the language in which those farmers talked to me about the things that have happened to their economy.
A great many pigs are produced up in the inter-lake country, and feed for them must be purchased. Of course the grain prices have disturbed the situation. I have a sheet here from a man who sent in five hogs. One of them graded as an A-l hog and the other four were too heavy. They were fifteen to twenty pounds too heavy. The packing company wrote a very nice letter saying that these were lovely hogs he sent in, lout they were a little too heavy. One of them was five pounds too heavy. But they said, "We have given you grade A-l for it," and that hog netted $36.25 for the farmer. The other four hogs were about twenty to twenty-five pounds too heavy and they averaged $2625 each. On five hogs that was a penalty of $50. I wonder whether the consumer got the benefit of that. I am sure that that procedure is not right. Nobody should make regulations that work against the farmer in that way. We know that if the farmer has a hog that is too heavy he should be penaliz-ed; but he should never be penalized to the extent of $10 a hog, because that is good pork. It may not be fit for Britain-
They would be glad to get it.

Yes, they would be glad to get it. The minister has been to Britain and has seen conditions. I have been there too and I have seen them. The people would be delighted to get the fat from the pig, let alone getting the bacon.
As I said when I started to talk about hogs, production is going down in my part of the country. From what I read in the papers, it is going down in other places as well. The reason is that the price of grain is putting everybody out of the hog-raising business. I have here a clipping from the Calgary Albertan, which has a paragraph headed "Dumping Hogs". It reads as follows:
Without exception, every hog producer spoken to is marketing his hogs as fast as possible. At an auction sale 12 miles east of here, weaner pigs, which two months ago would have been snapped up at six dollars or seven dollars each, sold for S5 cents each. A few days later, at another auction sale north of town, W'eaners and young feeder pigs of good quality did not get a bid. A farmer 20 miles southeast of here had 40 young pigs, and no feed to give them. He had expected to sell them to some of the larger feeders. Unable to dispose of them, he was forced to kill them all. Another farmer in town last week end, was approaching people on the street and in the stores, offering to give

them one, or more, or as many pigs as they would take, in order to get them off his own hands. One man made the prophecy that if something was not done within the next two weeks, by spring not one pig would be marketed from this entire area.
I believe that is what is happening all over. Quite close to where I myself farm, I know that pigs eight weeks old are being offered for fifty cents apiece. I have in my hand a letter from a man who finishes up by saying:
I kept fourteen sows myself. We raised one hundred pigs this year but by the first of January, 1948, we will not have one left.
I do not think I need to say any more to the minister. He realizes the seriousness of the situation, which has all been caused by this throwing of oats and barley on the speculative market where you do not know what you are going to pay; you do not know whether it will go up or down; it is at the mercy of the grain exchange. I thought the minister would know by this time that doing anything like that was not good for the agricultural economy of this country. The government never did that during the war because they could not afford to have any slip-up. It is just as essential now that we have a planned economy; in fact, it is more essential now than ever before.
Conditions are nearly as bad with the regard to the production of cattle. I have in my time kept quite a few cattle and worked with them. I have drawn the attention of the minister to the fact that the meat board gives that protection only when the animal is hung up. Of course I know what the minister's answer is. It is that if I want to have the meat board to take over my cattle, they will grade them. There is no one today in organized agriculture or in seventy-five per cent of agriculture who wants to hand over his cattle to the abattoir. Matters are altogether too definitely in the hands of the packer.
AVe read in the papers that the embargo may come off. I hope it does. I have asked for that for a long time. I asked for the temporary removal of it, and it may come. If it does come, I hope the meat board are there to accept the responsibility they should take. They should take the responsibility, with regard to the cattle that come there, of seeing that everybody gets a square deal. They should buy the animals on the hoof and ship them to the United States. If that is not done, only the big ranchers and the fellows who can ship carloads to the United States will be able to participate in that extra price. The small man, who has only half a dozen steers to come on the market, can not go to the United States because he is required to have a carload of cattle. If the embargo is

Agricultural Products Act
taken off, arrangements must be made for the meat board to go on the market to buy these cattle on the hoof and give that protection to the farmer.
The production of cattle has received a setback. People are talking about going out of the cattle-raising business. It is sometimes asked just how long we can stay in. I cannot speak about the big rancher. He raises cattle on a different 'basis from that on which my neighbours and I operate.
The question is often asked as to what the price of cattle should be in order to allow the farmer a labour return and a capital return, comparable with those of others who buy our products and whose products we buy. In order to answer this question we must first have knowledge of our costs. In consultation with men who should know a little better than I do-I give them credit for knowing more about it because they have been in the business longer than I have-I have worked out some figures.
Can one man working a forty or forty-four hour week for the six winter months look after a herd of thirty-five cattle? Of these, sixteen or seventeen would be cows, and thirteen or fourteen, young stock, also three or four heifers coming along to replace the cows, and a bull.
In order to bring them up to about 800 pounds each a person would have to feed each animal about a ton of grain, worth approximately $50 at today's prices. Each of the young stock would need at least a ton of good quality hay, worth about $15. This is a total of $65 for each of the fourteen young stock. Then the stock cattle would need at least thirty tons of hay at $15, which would amount to S450, as well as twenty or thirty loads of straw, worth about $2 a load. There would be pasture for the herd at $1 per month per head, including fencing, salt, taxes, providing a water supply, and so on, which would amount to $200.
Then we come to the overhead. The cattle would be worth about $3,000 and the barn another $3,000. This is an investment of $6,000. I do not think we would be asking too much if we expected to receive four per cent on that, which would be $240. People who do not have their money invested in cattle can get three per cent on government bonds, and they are guaranteed against the loss of either principal or interest. When the farmer needs capital he has to borrow from the banks at five per cent.
Depreciation, insurance, repairs on the barn and so on at five per cent would amount to $150. Maintaining a water supply, including 5849-29
well cost, gasoline, troughs and other things one needs would amount to $50. Then there is the bull cost, which would average about $3.50 per cow. Also there are veterinary costs, death and disease losses, tlhe cost of keeping a team to look after the cattle and so on, which is estimated at about $100.
This totals $2,200. In view of the fact that the farmer is a skilled workman-and I do not think anyone will deny that-he has to know more than the average man-and must be his own foreman and manager, it would seem that he should receive at least $40 a week for five months, which would be $800, bringing the total up to $3,000. Such a herd might be expected to have fourteen head of marketable cattle annually, weighing about 800 pounds each, or a total of 11,200 pounds of live cattle. With total costs of $3,000 the total cost per hundredweight on the farm would be $26.78. Freight and marketing costs would have to be added to this figure to arrive at the price where you are going to sell them. I think about the highest we are getting is $16.75, so that from these figures it will be seen that the farmer is not receiving wages, is not being allowed for his time and is not getting a return on his investment.
I do not want to take up any more time, but I think the minister will have to increase the prices for these products if we are to supply Britain with the food she needs. I think we should do so. We have a good bacon market there, and it would be too bad to lose it. Ours was the finest bacon going to Britain. It certainly lost its identity over there, but I had an opportunity of seeing the different grades of bacon they were receiving, and ours was away ahead of all the rest. We can send good beef also, we can help them in many ways, but we shall have to build up the confidence of our producers. We have destroyed the confidence of the farmer by getting out and getting in. We must have steady prices. If it was necessary to have a steady price for wheat for five years it is just as essential to have steady prices for cattle, sheep and hogs. You cannot interfere with the cost of the things that go into the production of these things, either, because if you do you change the whole situation.
I hope the minister will give us some good news before we go home. I hope he will increase these prices and give some promise of stability in connection with agricultural products.

You have already had news of the prices that are (to be paid.

I have not heard any
announcement as to price, unless you mean we are to get the same prices we received in the past.
No; I have said the prices are to be increased. It has been said at least four times, and I am sure everyone out in the country knows about it.
But will the quantities be reduced?

I do not want to break the rules, Mr. Speaker, but I should like to understand what the minister is saying. He says he has made the statement four times. I wish he would make it the fifth time, to see if I can catch it.
I have said the prices are to be increased to take care of the increased cost of feed grain.
How soon, and how much?
I am glad to hear that. I hope the increases will be sufficient, because if they are not you will never rest in your bed.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to say a few words before this motion is carried. I had hoped the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) would make a lengthy and complete statement on this question before this debate took place. From what he has said just now I am inclined to believe that, had he done so, the debate might have been shortened. He has just indicated that prices of meat products will be increased so that they will bear a fair relationship to the cost of the feeds that go into the raising of the livestock.
That is what was said 'n the statement made by the Prime Minister.

I am very glad the Minister of Agriculture has made this statement, because I have been reading the statement by the Prime Minister and, to be perfectly honest, I cannot find much in it. I have that statement in my hand at the moment. The other day I thought the Prime Minister made an outstanding statement, when he cautioned us in this house in regard to the speeches made by hon. members during the debate. In effect he said that if hon. members realized the serious condition in which the world finds itself today they might be a little more cautious in what they said and did. I attached a great deal of importance to that statement. Today the Prime Minister made

another statement, however, which in my opinion contradicts what he said previously.
The Minister of Agriculture has made reference to the statement made by the Prime Minister today. I should like also to refer to it for a moment. In the statement he made just a short time ago the Prime Minister pointed out, I think correctly, that we cannot continue indefinitely to export on credit and at the same time pay cash for the things we import.
That is what I said a long time ago.

It is strange that the government has not changed its policy so that when we export goods and services we shall import goods and services in exchange. I am glad the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) brought up that matter, because I am going to refer to it in just a moment. After having said that, the Prime Minister went on to say:
Both countries at the present time face a common difficulty, namely, a shortage of United States dollars. From the Canadian standpoint, this and other factors limit the extent to which the balance of the credit, provided for under the Financial Agreement Act of 1946, can be drawn on in order to make supplies available to the United Kingdom.
Apparently we are not going to make available to the United Kingdom all those things we could make available if w*e extended the production of this country. Apparently we are going to limit that assistance to the amount of credit balance upon which Great Britain is permitted to draw.
No.
That is what the Prime Minister was speaking about.
Read what it says.

I shall read it again:
Both countries at the present time face a common difficulty, namely, a shortage of United States dollars.
And then he goes on to say:
From the Canadian standpoint, this and other factors limit the extent to which the balance of the credit, provided for under the Financial Agreement Act of 1946, can be drawn on in order to make supplies available to the United Kingdom.
I imagine that "supplies" includes-
Read the first paragraph at the top of page 3, if the hon. member is talking about farm products.

I will come to that. The Prime Minister is there saying that supplies will be made available, and agricultural supplies will be included.

Agricultural Products Act
Before turning to other points, I should like to refer to one other part of the announcement. It will be noticed the Prime Minister emphasized that we are going to do everything we can to assist the United Kingdom, but that it depends entirely upon the credit balance upon which she is allowed) to draw. Then at page 2 he makes this statement:
However, though there may have been a shortage of dollars on both sides, there has been also on both sides a surplus of good will and mutual understanding.
That is very good; but the British people cannot live on good will and understanding- nor can anybody else. That is the trouble with the government's policy. They have expected the farmers of this country to carry on with good will and understanding, but with little cash in return for the goods they have produced, and the efforts they have put into the production of those goods.
As I go through the Prime Minister's speech, I find it is just a lot of pious platitudes which do not amount to very much at all, and I do not think I will spend more time on it.
I should like for a moment to speak more particularly about the matter under discussion, namely the Agricultural Products Act, which concerns generally agricultural production. I do not think there is anyone in the house, not even on the government side, who would dare contend for one moment that there is not great and widespread discontent throughout all the agricultural areas of Canada, among both the grain growers and the meat producers. It is a queer thing that we cannot now find sufficient incentive in this country to go ahead with an all-out production program. Wherever we turn in our agricultural program we find every effort is being made to curtail production. No doubt the reason for the curtailment of production is that the government, and particularly the Minister of Agriculture, is fearful lest the farmers raise too much of any one product so that they would1 not have a market for it.
I agree with him to the extent that we should not encourage farmers to raise more of one particular product to the detriment of another. But in this time of great scarcity when all the countries of Europe are clamouring so loudly for more food-to say nothing of their other necessities-we in Canada should be putting forth every effort possible to encourage our farmers to raise everything they can.
Instead of that, it was not so long ago that the federation of agriculture met the government here in Ottawa; and it was certainly stated in the press that the president of that 5849-29i
organization was advocating to the farmers that they should not increase the areas in wheat production. Because of the unsatisfactory wheat prices I believe the farmers will most definitely curtail their production, rather than enlarge it.
I should think every effort should be made to encourage the farmer to raise all the wheat and coarse grains possible. I believe there is just as great a need now for increased production of these commodities as there was in wartime.
We have heard hon. members from all sections of the house describe the destructive means used in reducing hog production; we have heard of the slaughter of young pigs and of brood sows being sent to the slaughterhouses. That is deliberate sabotage.
True.

This is particularly true when people in this country are living on a sub-standard level. Certainly one of our best markets is the market we have right here in Canada. I was amazed the other day when I heard one of the ministers say we could not consume all we produce in this country. In my view, the only logical market-perhaps I should say ultimate market-is with the Cana^ dian people themselves. No matter what we produce in Canada, or in what quantities, unless we wish to give it away we must ultimately consume it.
Someone will say, "If we have a surplus of
500.000.	000 bushels of wheat, after our own requirements are taken out, do you expect the people to glut themselves with that amount of wheat?" Of course not; no sensible person would say that. Then one would be asked, "What would you do with that surplus of
500.000.	000 bushels?" We would export them, and in return we would obtain imports of those goods which we cannot produce efficiently in this country. When those imports are received we must make it possible to effect distribution among our people so that they may consume them. Therefore indirectly we have the consumption of 500,000,000 bushels of wheat. Consequently it is absurd to say that we shall not consume everything we produce.
We have overlooked our greatest market, the one right here, and the consuming possibilities of the people of Canada. The higher we raise our standard of living, the greater will be our production and the greater the prosperity of our people; incidentally, the greater will be the prosperity of other countries wishing to have our surplus products. Apparently, however, the government does not yet realize that fact.
Agricultural Products Act

It seems criminal that in Canada we should tolerate a program of restricted production. It may be of interest to know that only a few evenings ago I was a guest at a Masonic dinner in Ottawa, and that during the evening some pictures which had been taken by Mayor Lewis of this city were shown. Those pictures had reference to his trip overseas of two or three months ago. There is nothing confidential or secret about them, because they were shown at an open dinner. While overseas, he took those pictures showing the deplorable conditions in European countries as a result of the war. Those conditions were certainly bad. The same picture has been drawn for us verbally in the house by the Prime Minister and on other occasions by others, and what has been said verified what was shown in the pictures.
I was amazed to note that, while these European countries were struggling to make a recovery, their recovery was very slow indeed. The destruction was great and their want was great. But when it came to Russia, particularly in Moscow, the recovery was exceptional; it was almost phenomenal. As the picture showe'd, they are taking great pains in Russia and are exercising special caution with regard to the health and training of their young people, and I emphasize the training angle. I cannot recall the exact percentage of our young men who were rejected as being physically unfit during the last war, but it was considerable. That condition had been brought about principally through malnutrition. We should be giving more consideration now to the health and welfare of our people because we do not know how soon we shall be calling upon our young people to fight another war for so-called freedom and democracy. We are permitting our people to exist at this time on a substandard level caused by high prices and curtailed production. We are heading into a period of scarcity. An article appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of December 16, 1947, reading as follows:
It is a tribute to Canada's wartime administration that, despite astronomical expenditures, there was comparatively little profiteering and that few "war millionaires" emerged from the last war.
That article may be right and there may have been only a few millionaires created. If my memory serves me aright, I think I saw a statement not long ago to the effect that only seven millionaires had emerged from the last war. A total of seven millionaires is not bad when we were told there was to be no profiteering. I think I am safe in saying that there were no millionaires created in the agricultural field. We should be developing a program
IMr. Johnston.]
which would be giving our farmers a fair return for the goods produced and for the effort put into producing their goods, so that there will be a closer relationship between the things which the farmer must sell and those which he must buy.
As far as the Agricultural Products Act is concerned, we have no objection to the continuance of its powers for the period desired by the government; that is, to March 31, 1948. I think it should be noted that apparently the only necessity of having this debate at this time is because of the government's, I was going to say fear, but perhaps that is not the proper term to use. Some people are saying that the only reason this session was called was to permit the government to have a caucus of its members. I am not saying that; that is just what has been indicated to me, but I cannot see any better reason for it. There was no necessity of calling parliament to renew this act because it would have gone over automatically until March 31 had the government not been so anxious in other directions to have parliament called.
I can see nothing in the act that we would object to; in fact we will agree to having it extended for the required time. Personally I cannot see that there is great importance to be attached to the act. It is true that it does give the government power, if it wishes to use it, to sell or export agricultural products, and no one -has objection to that. The act also sets up commodity boards through which this purchase and sale may be made under the instructions and control of the minister.
This particular act is closely associated with the Agricultural Prices Support Act, to which I will refer later on. That act is referred to specifically in section 4 (2) of this act. Then, under section 5, people raising agricultural products can be required 'to deliver them for sale or for export. That is one good part of the act because it makes it possible for these prices to be based on the proper contract price and bear a reasonable relationship thereto. I think thait section would give the government sufficient power to create a fair relationship between the cost of coarse grains and the prices which farmers receive for meat products. In my view, that will have to be fairly substantial. I do not think a ten per cent rise in the price will create a fair relationship between the selling price of coarse grains and the present price of meat products.

The ante will have to be
raised.

The hon. member for
Battle River suggests that we shall have to raise the ante quite a little bit. When the

Agricultural Products Act
minister makes his statement I hope he will tell us that the ante is being raised.
I wanted to refer to the Agricultural Prices Support Act. I think that is a rather good act and I am referring to it because it must be taken in conjunction with this act. The only complaint I have to make thus far is that the government has definitely neglected to use the power given in this act. If we extend the provisions of the Agricultural Products Act to March 31 I do not think it will make any great difference in the price structure of agricultural goods because the government will follow the same policy in the future as it has done in the past. That power has been there ever since the act was put into effect and yet nothing has been done about it.
Section 9, subsection 1 of the Agricultural Prices Support Act gives the government the power to set prices, but I think it is correct to say that when a price is set it would not act as a ceiling price; it would be definitely a floor price. However, they could at least raise up t'he floor price so that it would insure agriculture a fair return for the coarse grains and meat products the farmers have to sell. Paragraph (c) of subsection 1 of section 9 provides for the payment of subsidies to producers. It reads:
(c) to pay to the producers of an agricultural product directly or through such agent as the board may determine the difference between a price prescribed by the board with the approval of the governor in council for such product and the average price, as determined by the board, at which such product is sold in the market during a specified period if such average price is below such prescribed price.
There is no difficulty there in the government extending the principle of subsidy payments. I was interested in hearing the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) advocate a moment ago an increase in the price of agricultural products. He pointed out the different items which entered into the cost of production, but he did not think that, even though other factors were considered, there should be a rise in the price to the consumer. I think I am interpreting his remarks correctly. Of course that could be handled under the provisions of this paragraph by the payment of a subsidy. That is why I think this section should be carried out.
Then, under subsection 2 of section 9, the government is given the power to set parity prices. The subsection reads:
In prescribing prices under paragraphs (a) and (c) of subsection one of this section, the board shall endeavour to ensure adequate and stable returns for agriculture by promoting orderly adjustment from war to peace conditions and shall endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns from agriculture and those from other occupations.
If that power were used and that principle followed, then I do not think agriculture would have any complaint. But most certainly that power has never been used and that principle has never been followed because agriculture has never received its fair share of the national revenue. I think it was from 1915 to 1919 that the industry of agriculture received its fair share of the national income.
When I speak of a parity price, perhaps it would be well that I should define the term lest the government would not understand what it is. I would say that the farmers are receiving a parity price when the price which they receive for their production bears the same relation to the value of the national production as the farm population bears to the national population. If that principle were followed I am sure that agriculture would do more than its share in increasing production. But if that principle is not acted upon, most assuredly agriculture will do the same as industry would do, and I would not blame them for it; that is, they will not produce the goods if they cannot receive a fair return for their labours.
A word about the handling of coarse grains. It is true that we have a wheat board which handles all Canadian wheat, and the government said that it wished to ensure a fairly stable price during the five-year period when the contracts with Britain were in force. I am not going to praise the contracts with Britain. I think they were wrong in some respects. I think the application of the whole principle was wrong. But I do think the handling of wheat through the wheat board was a good thing. The hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) indicated, in his remarks in the house on Thursday, December 11, our attitude with regard to coarse grains. It is my view that coarse grains should be handled through the wheat board. I am unalterably opposed to the continuation of the Winnipeg grain exchange. I cannot see any good that they have rendered in the past, except perhaps to line their own pockets to the detriment of agriculture. My belief is that agriculture would be satisfied with a long-term arrangement whereby the farmers would get decent and fair returns for their products. I do not think they would be satisfied with anything less, nor do I think they should be satisfied with anything less.
We have a meat board, and I think there should be very close co-operation between the meat board and the wheat board, if the wheat board is to handle coarse grains. The minis-
Agricultural Products Act

ter himself indicated a while ago that there should be a fair relationship between the price of meat products and the price of feed grains. It goes without saying that that is a sound principle. I trust that he will carry out that principle and I shall be watching him closely to see if that is done. But it cannot be done unless there is close co-operationi between the meat board and the wheat board, which we hope will handle coarse grains.
I am going to suggest to the house something which I think is new in regard to trade agreements, particularly as they apply to agricultural products. In making agreements on an international basis for the interchange of goods and services in order to put our export trade on a more firm foundation, one which would be fair and equitable, not only to Canada as an exporting country, but to those countries which are compelled or desire to import our products, we believe that a national products marketing act should be passed whereby long-term agreements with other countries could be negotiated in such a manner as to ensure a fair and stable price structure in Canada. First, a parity price should be established in Canada for agricultural products, and I have already indicated what I mean by a parity price. Then the export price-and this is the important part- which is agreed to in the international agreement should be tied to the price level of the country with which the agreement is made in order to ensure a proper trade relationship between the contracting parties. There would then not be the danger of fluctuations from time to time which would upset the contract. Suppose the price level in the importing countries should rise by ten per cent; then the price set in the agreement should also rise by ten per cent. In that way a constant relationship would automatically be maintained between the volume of imports and the volume of exports. That would make effective the suggestion which was made by one of our members a while ago, that now, particularly when Great Britain is in such dire need of such goods and services as we have to offer, the flow of those goods and services should not be impeded by the extent to which those other countries lack access to United States dollars. It seems a terrible tragedy that when the country is in such a critical condition as that in which we find ourselves today, almost as critical as in 1939, we should hesitate in any way to hasten the reconstruction of Great Britain and other European countries and not supply them with the food and necessities which they need. The times are so urgent that I think the government

should revise its policy of restricted production in agriculture and encourage maximum production in all lines, having in mind, of course, a reasonable production program. Agriculture should be paid according to the services it renders, and the farmers should receive fair returns for the things they have to sell in comparison with the prices they have to pay for the things they have to buy.

Mr. Speaker, I have just listened with considerable interest to t'he hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston), and I am sure that few could take exception to much that he said. I think we all share the general objective of a prosperous agriculture in Canada, and I believe it is generally conceded that the greatest market we have for our agricultural products is our own home market. For many years the party to which I have the honour to belong have felt that the development of industry in Canada, with increased employment and increased purchasing power in the hands of the people, would mean, in the end, increased prosperity for agriculture. I am glad that I can agree with the hon. member for Bow River in that and also with many other statements that he made in regard to the present situation in the markets of the world. But I am not altogether in agreement with him in what he said as to conditions overseas. He said that His Worship Mayor Lewis of Ottawa painted a very favourable picture of Russia. Not long ago I was within sound of the rattle of the iron curtain and the reports that I heard-
I only mentioned Russia to show where we were lagging.

I understand that he meant
to show how the few in Russia who were fed were fed scientifically. I regret to say I have heard that more people have starved to death in Russia in the last few years than our total population. However, that is Russia's business, and I am sure the hon. member for Bow River only wished to point out that there have been some scientific methods, even in Russia.
I feel, sir, that the motion before t'he house calls for some comment. It is a rather strange one. It is another novel illustration of the futility of this session itself. When you stop to think, you realize that this motion is in exactly the same terms as the motion with respect to emergency powers. The motion is that, whereas section 11 of the Agricultural Products Act, being chapter 10 of the statutes of 1947, provides that, subject as thereinafter

Agricultural Products Act
provided, that act shall expire on December 31, if parliament meets during November or December; if parliament does not so meet it shall expire on the sixtieth day after parliament first meets in 1948, or on March 31.
There you have another example of the government asking the house to solve a problem which the convening of parliament has itself created. We have started almost everything and finished nothing except the birthday celebration yesterday of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). That is the only thing that has been successful. With unanimity the house honoured the right hon. gentleman, and it was quite delightful. Let me say in all seriousness, Mr. Speaker, that I am a farmer and you are a lawyer; there are other things that I can do, just as there are things elsewhere that you can attend to, and the only benefit I see either for myself or my constituency has been in the fact that I was honoured in being here and spending that pleasant hour with the genial Prime Minister on his seventy-third birthday. I hope he will live long enough to see a government in power which will re-establish free enterprise in this country.
There are many sides to this issue. For many years we on this side of the 'house, and many members on the other side as well, have emphasized the need of a balanced agricultural economy, and we Rave heard for many years about world markets, how to get them and retain them and what they would mean to the general prosperity of Canada. I think it is only reasonable to say that we all now full}' understand, as many of us indeed have pointed out, that if food were necessary to win the war it will go a long way toward winning the peace.
As you know, Mr Speaker, the world today is hungry and cold, even in the old land, and we have, I believe, an obligation in Canada to produce to the maximum in order to help to feed the hungry children of Europe and especially of the United Kingdom A strong Canadian agriculture is therefore a vital necessity for world prosperity if we are to avert the catastrophe that lies ahead and stave off the possibility of another war or the development of those socialistic trends that have brought Europe to the brink of ruin. If we are to do that, Canadian agriculture is challenged as no other industry in the country, indeed no other industry in the world, is challenged today.
I say, therefore, that it goes much farther than a question of profits which the farmer will receive for his products. So long as we have this system of payment for services, the so-called profit system, then, as the member for
Bow River said, the incentive to production is the spark and the creative impulse that will give us the necessary production to meet the challenge.
I know that the government now in power as well as the party it represents have for many years emphasized in this house time and again that it was their objective to find markets throughout the world. I recall how, in the years gone by, they said they would search Europe for new markets.
That was Bennett.

I see you are getting on with your correspondence. You did not hear what I said. I can recall that hon. gentlemen opposite said that they would broaden markets for our Canadian products. That was what we heard from the present Prime Minister and the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) as well as from many of the other senior members of that party. They emphasized that while this party stood for the protection of industry, for the development of industry and increasing employment here in Canada and building up home markets, Canadian agriculture must depend on markets far off for their surplus products.
As the hon. member for Bow River has said we are now approaching the time when our people will be able to consume what we can produce. We can consume a great proportion of our total production. Apart from wheat, I believe that if the people of Canada were allowed to obtain all the food they wanted, and if they maintain normal purchasing power, their consumption would be close to our total production of food.
We know now what happened some years ago. We are discovering the uncertainty of foreign markets, even in the United Kingdom. In my opinion, we have an obligation, apart from the question of maintaining markets in the world for our foodstuffs, to assist the motherland in the difficulties she is in at the present time. But some months ago, among the many problems that faced the farmer as well as the Minister of Agriculture, some of which the minister met and some of which he helped to create before he met them, we found that the farmer, instead of producing more hogs, was selling his breeding stock. As the hon. member for Bow River has just said, and there is not a representative of rural riding who does not realize it-small pigs are being destroyed.
Let me tell the Minister of Agriculture that in western Ontario it was reported the other day that a farmer drove into a town with a small half-ton truck in which he had seventeen pigs for sale. He left them and went to dinner,
Agricultural Products Act

and when he came back there were forty-seven pigs in the truck, which is some indication of the popularity of the program.
There were more little pigs the last time I heard that story.

It must be true if you heard it too. The Prime Minister has presented us with an attractive document in which we are assured that everything will be all right for the farmer. There is no more uncertainty. He can keep his brood sows three months longer anyway. The Prime Minister has assured the farmer that there is a surplus of good will and mutual understanding in the old land. He says that dollars are short in the United Kingdom and admits they are about as short here, and they are getting shorter every day, by the way. Then emphasis is placed on the necessity for Canada to maintain a balanced agricultural economy.
That is a delightful program. I have been listening to spokesmen of the government, and I have gathered the impression that they themselves really believe that every time they set up a target they hit a bull's-eye. It is a matter of pious hopes and purposes that anybody could suggest. The hon. member for Bow River made reference to this document. The minister says to read at the top of page 3.
I shall do so. It states:
Canada wishes to continue to send to the United Kingdom all those supplies of foodstuffs and raw materials which are playing such a vital part in sustaining the United Kingdom's reconstruction program. The United Kingdom's need for such supplies, in order to maintain the progress now visible in her recovery, is so strong and compelling that any interruption at this time would have very serious consequences.
That is a fine paragraph. It is well written and it was equally well read. The Minister of Agriculture explained it. There is nothing in this document, Mr. Speaker, and there is less in the explanation of the Minister of Agriculture. All it says is that the agreement we now have will be carried on for three months.
No. no; for a year.
That it will be carried on for a year, yes. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture had better get together. The Prime Minister said you are going to review it in three months.
No, not those agreements.
What agreements are you talking about?
He is talking about credit arrangements.

Mr. Speaker, may I say to the minister that I could make his speech but I 
do not want him to make mine. I cannot understand how the Minister of Agriculture, or even the more imaginative Prime Minister, can hope the farmers will get much comfort out of this, or that any hon. member of this house will do so either. The minister has been asked repeatedly this afternoon how soon we shall be told, and how much. He has been asked what quantities we are going to sell and how much we are going to receive for them. In his statement this afternoon, the Minister of Agriculture has admitted that he is not yet sure of the quantity and he is not sure of the price. He does not know yet. But he says, in view of their record of keeping the balance maintained in relation to feed grains cost, everyone in Canada pretty well knows what it will be. Well, I have been farming for a long time and I have taken a great many risks; but I certainly would not want to take the risk of speculating on what this government might do next with reference to prices.
With regard to this statement which is made after three months' negotiation with the British authorities, I suggest that there is nothing in it that an intelligent minister of the British government and an intelligent minister of this government could not find out and on which they could not make a report like this in three minutes, because there are no quantities mentioned. The wheat agreement is continued. There were no quantities mentioned in the others. However, there is one encouragement in it, and that is that the Minister of Agriculture is more cautious in suggesting quantities with regard to all the other articles except wheat. In fact, I believe that none of the quantities which were mentioned a year or two ago have been fulfilled. The only contract, other than the wheat contract, that we have lived up to with Britain is the one on dehydrated milk. I am not sure whether that one has been carried out in full or not, but I understand it has been almost so.
I do not intend to review what has been so well said by the former speaker as to the loss the Canadian poultry man has endured, the discouragement to the Canadian hog man and to livestock producers in general. But it does appear to me that this half-hearted and half-baked plan which has been instituted by this government has done more to discourage the agricultural production we might have had than any other single factor. I know that later on today the Minister of Agriculture will say, "Compare our production with that back in the years 1920 and 1930. Compare our prices with those of 1930. Compare our prices with the prices received in the days of the

Agricultural Products Act
Bennett government. Compare national production. Compare our industrial production. Compare our national revenue." Yes, Mr. Speaker, compare the taxes that we are paying. There are many other comparisons that we can make. The farmer today is paying for a costly, novel experiment that this government is carrying on; and I say again that it is a half-hearted and half-baked socialistic planning pjogram for agriculture. If they would get together with their other socialistic friends in the C.C.F. party in this house, they might have it fully-tbaked and more whole-hearted. The only way one can distinguish them in the country now is as Liberal socialists and C.C.F. socialists. The C.C.F. socialists say they would return to wartime control. As I observe their absence, they must be holding a caucus. I wish some of them would tell me if they would return to a wartime economy with fixed prices and price ceilings, as they have stated, would they fix wages as well? I should like to ask some of them if they would put a rigid ceiling on wages today.
You were told that before.
Will you tell me again?
The answer is, no.
No. You would allow the farmers' wages to go up but you would put a price ceiling on other products, would you?
Yes.

That would be fine. That is half-baked. It is about the same as the others. They would put a price ceiling on what the farmer has to sell, but they would not put any price ceiling on the wages he has to pay or the goods he buys. So they at least would get perhaps half of the support and the chances are they may not even get that. But, Mr. Speaker, I think the government have been busy in keeping prices down. I have never known such a diligence to keep prices down in the history of this country. I have certainly never known it in my experience in this house, which has covered a considerable number of years; and if I have my health I hope it will continue. I do not know, but perhaps I may have enough friends such as the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) or the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) or somebody else who will soon be placing roses around my desk, as I should like to place them around theirs, for long service in this house.
It all depends on you.

I have never known any minister to be so diligent for such a long time in trying to keep agricultural prices down. Never in the history of this country has the farmer carried such a load as he is carrying in this expensive experiment to which he is the chief contributor. When one stops to think of it, he realizes that we are, with pride, telling about the renewal of the wheat agreements at the same price, but that the farmer has been receiving for that wheat one-half of the world price. Hundreds of millions of dollars could have been in circulation in this country had we been receiving world prices. Talk about stability or security for the future! It is like taking out. an insurance policy where, the insurance agent asks you not only to pay the premium, but to pay the whole policy in advance. The farmer has carried the load all through. In all fairness, if the minister of agriculture has these socialistic brain waves, and wants to try them out, and use the farmer more or less as a guinea pig, and make agriculture the loss leader in this new-fangled economy, it seems to me that all should pay for it. I do not think the farmers of Canada should endure the burden of the millions of dollars required to try out this experiment. If we are to continue to follow this doctrine; if we believe that we should give the United Kingdom wheat at half the world price and that the farmers should be asked to take $150,000,000 or perhaps $200,000,000 less than world prices would give them, let us go the whole way. Let the national economy of this country take over the burden of our debt of gratitude to the old country, so that it will be distributed over all the taxpayers. Is that not fair? Probably if the farmers were better organized they would be better heard.
I say, in all sincerity, that the farmers of this country, like everyone else, are frightened at such novel state planning. They are frightened by the government's failure to give them any incentive to remain in the hog business. Many poultrymen are 'being frightened out of business in this country. No one knows what he will get in future. Even the Minister of Agriculture says he does not know. He is going to give them something, but he does not know how much. He is going to fix it for a year; he is going to relate the increase to the costs of grain, which are rising steadily. I dio not know whether it will be fixed for a full year or whether it will be a New Year's present to the farmers, or a Christmas present, or perhaps an Easter present. Perhaps by Easter the prices of feed grain will be still higher. We understand that these agreements were to provide stability for many years;
Agricultural Products Act

instead, in the few months they have been in effect they have created more uncertainty than anything in the history of Canadian agriculture.
If our home markets mean a great deal, as they do, what will happen to them from all the insecurity that has been created by some of the recent moves of this government? I am not going to review them, but we all know the effects of some legislation that has been passed, and we know the effects of the additional excise tax, which has been imposed without legislation. In many cases this excise tax on home production will put local producers out of business. There are young returned men in this country who have invested every dollar of their gratuities and who are on the verge of losing everything. Why? I know the ex-Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) would reply, "Well, you know the reason. We need more United States dollars, and we must hang on to the few we still have". We have allowed nearly all our United States exchange to slip away. Perhaps the minister would admit, though so far no member of the cabinet has been bold or honest enough to admit it, that some bureaucratic economists have advised1 that the dollar should be raised every time we get into a position like this. Perhaps some of these days they may put it up to SI.10. On that point I will only say that whoever is to blame has created a situation which is not only prejudicing agriculture but is creating uncertainty and ruining industry in this country as well. Prophecies are dangerous things, perhaps, and especially here; but I venture to predict that, before three months have passed, the dollar will be back at ninety cents. If it were not for Bret-ton Woods it would go even farther, because its honest value is not $1, as no one knows better than the government of the day.
As I mentioned at the outset, Mr. Speaker, it has been the policy of the party to your right, since before you and I were born, to search the world for markets for our agricultural products. If I have heard it said in this house once I have heard it a hundred times, that the only way we could hope to sell our great agricultural surpluses was by being ready to buy. That is why we who sit to your left were condemned for a quarter of a century for being strongly in favour of developing industry in Canada, of maintaining protective tariffs, high protection, if you like. But we certainly never established prohibition, as it has been established by those who sit to your right. Why are they doing that? Because of the shortage of United States dollars. I suggest that even this has been clumsily

muddled. If this government were forced to keep United States dollars here in Canada, the few that are left to us, why did they not say to all the importers, "We will allow you to buy only eighty per cent of the things you have been allowed to buy in the past from outside." Then they would not have put Jones out of business and left Smith in business; they would not have given an advantage to one returned soldier and put another at a disadvantage. They would not have put people out of business entirely, as their folly now is doing. I throw that out only as a suggestion. The government may not consider it constructive, but at least it is not as destructive as the policies now in vogue.
I should like the government to answer a question. I hope the Minister of Agriculture will answer it; he can always give an answer, whether or not it is right. When he speaks I hope he will tell us how we can expect to maintain those markets in Britain if the old doctrine is still true that we must buy if we hope to sell. How can we hope to sell to Britain when we tell her we are going to buy less? We are putting restraints and prohibitions on our trade with the United States because we are buying more from her than we are selling. By the way, since 1900 we have bought about forty or fifty billion dollars worth more from the United States than we have sold her.
