They had a margin of five cents, or whatever it was, between the floor and ceiling prices within which they could operate; and they did operate. So that the grain exchange has not -been closed.
I just wanted to make that statement. As proof, I would refer to rye, which has been running up and down during the whole period.
You might add that the dominion government does not. have the power to close the exchange.
That is right.

Then I am going to ask the minister this further question. Would he consider placing all coarse grains under the wheat board? That has been suggested to me by the farmers of my constituency, and it is another of the questions to which I should like to take back an answer.

Then may I answer
that question, just in a few words? The question as to whether the grain exchange can be closed is one which will have to be settled by this house. There is at present no legislation which permits the government to close it, and I am not too sure that we can deal with it ourselves.
As regards the other question, as to what I think about coarse grains being placed under the wheat board, that, too, is something which must be decided by the house. We have no authority at present under the wheat board act to place coarse grains under the wheat board. That question was discussed last session, and I took it	from	the	discussionwhich then took	place	that	the	majorityof members were	opposed to	it.	However,
it may be discussed again during this session; and whatever decision the house reaches will be followed by the minister responsible for the administration of the Wheat Board Act.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The hon. member asked
your opinion.

Have the farmers of
your constituency	asked	that	coarse grains
be placed under the wheat board because they produce them, or because they hope to get them cheaper?

I am very glad the hon.
member asked that question, because it brings

Agricultural Products Act
up what appears to be a conflict of opinion existing between some of those on the prairies who produce the wheat and those in other provinces who buy it. I do not know if the hon. member agrees with me when I say that while, to a certain extent, although not altogether, your economy is tied up with export prices, rather it is tied up with those of us in this country who have to buy your grain. And while we on the Pacific coast are very glad to see the farmers in the prairie provinces getting all they should for their grain-and we have never begrudged them their price at all-on the other hand, we do not want the farmers in the prairie provinces to do that and then object because we come here and ask for increased prices for our eggs and poultry. We are buyers of grain, and we buy a great deal of it from the prairie provinces, particularly Alberta. I would ask the hon. member to give some thought for the welfare of the man who depends for his livelihood upon purchasing grain for the production of eggs, poultry and hogs.

Is the answer that
your farmers hope to buy more cheaply?

We want to buy grain as
cheaply as we can, or sell our products to meet the high prices you are charging. I think that is a fair answer to make.

Your answer is clear
enough. You want to buy it cheaper.

I think you put it very well.
Perhaps I am wrong, but it would seem you want to soak us all you can, and give nothing in return. I may be wrong, but when the hon. member challenges me, then I have a perfect right to interpret his question as I see it.
I asked only a simple question.
I shall be glad to answer any question you wish to ask.

I would ask hon. members not to interrupt the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) who has the floor, without asking his permission. I would remind hon. members that on this motion hon. members are allowed to speak only once.
'Mr. REID: You, Mr. Speaker, must perforce keep the rules; but these interjected questions do not worry me one bit. While we were pleased to hear that a settlement had been reached regarding beef, bacon, cheese and eggs may I suggest to the Minister of Agriculture that he give some thought to placing a floor under the price of poultry.
Nothing was mentioned about poultry, but it is the opinion of people in British Columbia that this should be done under the act already in force.
Are those double-breasted turkeys?
I am glad also that question was asked.
It gets you out of the other one, does it not?

I do not want to get out of any question; and if we had the time and the rules would permit, nothing would give me greater pleasure than to take on anyone-one at a time, of course-and answer all these questions; because, after being in public life for more than 25 years, the questions do not bother me very much. But, speaking of turkeys-
I was thinking about those big turkeys.

Those British Columbia turkeys with big breasts. There are two or three cars rolling all the way from British Columbia, and I advise you to taste them. After you do, you will always want British Columbia turkeys-just as the Ontario people want British Columbia apples, after tasting them. However, that brings something else into the discussion. One could have a real argument on that point.
I would ask the Minister of Agriculture to give thought to putting a floor under poultry. Realizing the time at our disposal is short and that many other members may wish to take part in the debate, I shall not take all the forty minutes at my disposal. I thought, however, it was my duty to bring to the attention of the minister the serious state of affairs confronting the poultrymen of British Columbia.
I should like now, for a moment or two, to refer to another industry, which has not been mentioned thus far in the discussions on the British trade agreements. I refer to the canned salmon situation. Speaking roughly, the average pack of canned salmon in British Columbia ranges from 1,300,000 cases to 2,000,000 cases a year. The industry is geared to put out a pack of a minimum of 1,000,000 cases. Prior to the war, we were supplying Great Britain with about 400,000 cases a year and provided the Canadian people with about
600,000	cases. Generally a million cases were divided between British and Canadian peoples in the amounts I have mentioned. Then the war came along and Great Britain said to our government, "We would like to have all
Agricultural Products Act

the canned fish you can produce." Our industry therefore geared up a little higher and supplied the British people during the war years with all the canned salmon we in British Columbia produced. The Canadian people willingly and gladly forewent that beautiful, lovely tasting sockeye salmon, and other varieties as well, so that the British people would be able to carry on and be fed.
Naturally we lost some markets thereby. Then, toward the end of the war, indeed as late as last year, the British ministry of food, which had a contract under which it agreed to take forty per cent of the canned salmon pack of British Columbia, asked the industry if it would be good enough to relinquish the agreement entered into. The industry agreed and said, "Yes, we will allow you to change the contract from forty per cent to twenty per cent of our pack".
Of that twenty per cent which we agreed to supply them, agreeing at the same time to find a market elsewhere for the remainder, thus far they have taken up only six per cent. They must have funds somewhere, because they would never have agreed to take twenty per cent of the entire canned salmon pack of British Columbia unless they knew they had th funds to pay for it, either through a loan from us or through their own efforts under their own financial economy.
We are now faced, however, with a loss of that market under the Geneva trade treaties, treaties which, by the way, few members have had time to study fully. All we can do at the moment is to take a salient point or article of the treaty here and there and give it some study. In fact the agreement is so voluminous no one needs apologize for not knowing the full import of its ramifications.
When the trade treaty was being negotiated those who were there representing the fishing industry overlooked one little point in connection with the exportation of fresh and frozen fish. The general meaning of fresh fish is fish that is caught and shipped direct to' the market in its fresh form, to be used in that form. Frozen fish is similar, only it is frozen to keep it longer and from deteriorating. It was never realized at the time that fresh fish would be exported to the United States to be processed into canned salmon.
On a point of order, I was wondering what fish have to do with the Agricultural Products Act. Are they to be used as fertilizer?
I did not quite understand the reason for the hon. member's first question, but when, in debate, an hon. member asks such a question now-well, it speaks for itself.
May I have your ruling, Mr. Speaker?

Since the debate started on the motion now before the house, the Speaker has been most generous to members on all sides. I would ask the hon. member to do everything possible to keep the debate relevant to the motion.

I am glad to see that you have the Christmas spirit, Mr. Speaker, but I do . not like to see it exhibited so freely by some members of the opposition.
If fish caught in British Columbia waters are to be bought up by the United States industry, the entire canning industry of that province will be in jeopardy and might very well be put completely out of business. I am glad the new Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Gregg) is with us tonight. I know he has this matter in hand and I draw his attention particularly to this point.
After all, something is owed to us by the British government and the British people. It is a little disquieting to learn that they are negotiating with a country, which only recently acquired fisheries, for something like
750,000	cases of salmon. I think it should be pointed out to them just what the Canadian people and the Canadian fishing industry did during the years of war. They should be asked to consider that. If they do that, then they will be following out the words used by the Prime Minister this afternoon when he said that the spirit of good will prevailed in the negotiations.
If they approach the matter from that point of view I am sure that they will give an order to this country for at least 200,000 cases of salmon. If not, I am afraid that the industry in British Columbia will suffer a collapse. I make no apology for drawing the attention of the house to this matter. It is a serious one, and I felt that it was my duty, representing as I do, not only an agricultural riding, but a riding where there are fishermen dependent upon the canning industry for their living, to bring this matter to the attention of the government and to urge that they make further representations to the British along the lines I have just suggested.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to delay the house very long in discussing this matter; but, coming as I do from an agricultural constituency and an agricultural province, I thought I should say a few words. I know the announcement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) this afternoon will be of great interest, not only to all members of this house, but to the people of Canada from one end to the

Agricultural Products Act
other. However, I do not think the Prime Minister gave us the information which we would have liked to have. He told us that the contract had been made and that agreements have been settled with Great Britain, but we do not know the nature of that contract. I do not feel that I can discuss at any length a contract the terms of which are not known to this house or to the people of Canada.
At the outset, I should like to ask the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) if it is a fact that definite contracts have been signed between Great Britain and Canada without prices being mentioned. As we all know, when a contract is made even between two individuals the price of the article being bought or sold is the very essence of the contract. Can the minister tell us whether prices have been stipulated in these contracts?

The prices which it is considered should be in the contract have been discussed with the representatives of the British who are here and those prices have been submitted to London for their consideration. We expect word very shortly with regard to them. The principle upon which those prices are to be arrived at has been settled. The principle is that there are to be increases over and above the prices which are now in the agreements to take care of what is considered to have been an increase in cost brought about by increases in grain prices not already taken care of.
That is about as indefinite as what we had before; there is nothing defin-nite about that.
There are several members over there who could figure it very quickly.

I think they would be guessing. As a matter of fact you have to do a lot of guessing when you ask questions of the government.
As I said, it is not my intention to take up much of the time of the house. I listened to the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) speak this afternoon. He emphasized a principle which he considered to be very important; that is, if we sell goods to Great Britain on credit, why should it be necessary for us to pay cash for the goods we buy from them?
It occurs to me that there are many things produced in England which we could use. For many years England has been the best customer of Canada and today she is producing goods which could be exchanged for
goods produced here. I do not think it is altogether necessary for us to pay cash to Great Britain for goods purchased there. I think the people of Great Britain would be most anxious to exchange goods with us. I should like to quote from a Canadian Press dispatch from London, dated December 16, and headed, "Meet Canadian Terms, News-Chronicle's Plea", and reading as follows:
"We hope very much that Britain will do her utmost to meet the Canadians," the paper said, adding that Canada has planned her "whole agricultural program to meet the needs of the British market."
It goes on to say:
In return, Canada should speedily discuss with Washington the raising of the embargo upon British imports which she imposed because she had to stop her purchases of United States goods and did not feel free to discriminate in favour of Britain.
Here is the last paragraph, which is the most important:
It is both tragic and absurd that there should be reports of clothing and textiles piling up unsold in British warehouses when it is known that Canada needs goods of this kind.
My point is this, that if there are goods piling up in Great Britain which Canada needs it is not fair to the Canadian people or to the people of Great Britain that we should impose an embargo upon British goods, especially when Great Britain is willing to exchange those goods for our farm products.
But my chief object tonight is to bring to the attention of the house the situation of agriculture in the maritime provinces. Agriculture is one of the great basic industries of the province of New Brunswick, and we have had a very difficult time in past years. During the war, while it was more difficult for us to produce in New Brunswick than in other parts of Canada, we did produce large quantities of agricultural products and our farmers in the province enjoyed a certain amount of prosperity. But within the last few weeks a situation has arisen in that province which is worse, I think, than in any other part of Canada, with the exception of our sister maritime provinces. In my own county of Kings, New Brunswick, dairying is carried on to a large extent; in fact, the town of Sussex, my home town, is known as the dairy centre of the maritime provinces. The fact remains, Mr. Speaker, that today many of our dairy herds of great value are being broken up and sold in that part of the country, and in addition, as has been pointed out by many other hon. members, hundreds of young pigs are being killed. I received a
Agricultural Products Act

letter just today from one of my constituents, in which he says:
For instance, I raised six choice young pigs from a fall litter, but as the price of the feed would come to more than the pigs would be worth after they had reached maturity I was forced to knock them on the head.
I am also killing off my hens as eggs will not pay the feed bill.
He mentions many other matters. The situation of that farmer is duplicated practically all over my constituency and in the province of New Brunswick.
To show hon. members just how much greater a burden our farmers in New Brunswick have to bear, I wish to quote from the Live Stock Market Review, of the Department of Agriculture, of December 11, 1947, in which a table is given showing millfeed prices in various parts of Canada. In Ontario and Quebec, with the exception of Riviere du Loup, which is in the constituency of the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) and for which at one time he got a railway station after strenuous efforts, the price of bran is $46.25; in Fredericton, New Brunswick, the price is $49.25, and in Antigonish, Nova Scotia, $50425.
Shorts is another feed used by many of our dairymen. It is selling at $47.50 in Ontario and Quebec, $50.50 in Fredericton, and $51.50 in Antigonish.
Middlings is selling at $51.50 in Ontario and Quebec, $54.50 in Fredericton, and $55.50 in Antigonish.
Barley meal is selling at $66.80 in Ontario and Quebec, $69.80 in Fredericton, and $70.80 in Antigonish.
Oat chop is selling at $67.50 in Ontario and Quebec, $70.50 in Fredericton and $71.50 in Antigonish.
Hon. members speak of the great difficulties which their farmers are having in other parts of Canada, but the millfeed prices which I have just put on Hansard show the added costs to which the farmers of the maritime provinces are put.
One of the great crops in New Brunswick is the potato crop. We have had a very good crop this year. I know the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Hatfield) will tell the house more about that. But an added difficulty in raising potatoes in New Brunswick is the great increase in the price of fertilizer in that province. I have here a Canadian Press dispatch from Ottawa, which, under the heading "Higher fertilizer price for maritime farmers next spring, says Ottawa" states:
A 20 per cent jump in fertilizer prices in the maritime provinces next spring was predicted today by the dominion Department of Agricul-

ture in a report placed before the opening meeting of the dominion-provincial agricultural conference.
The article goes on to state that the maritime provinces have the longest and most expensive freight haul from the sources of supply of fertilizer and that it is possible that price increases in the spring of 1948 will approximate eight per cent in Ontario, twelve per cent in Quebec, and twenty per cent in the maritime provinces. Other members think their farmers are having a difficult time, but I would ask them if the plight of their farmers would not be much worse if they had to pay the increased costs that our farmers in the maritime provinces have to pay.
I am sorry to see that no provision is made in the agreements for the sale of apples. Under the British empire trade agreements, the apple industry in Nova Scotia flourished to an extent that it never did before, and ships were specially constructed, I believe, to convey our apple crop from the maritimes and Canada to Great Britain. During the war it was fairly easy for us in the maritimes to dispose of our apple crop through making apple cider, apple juice and by processing apples. But that should not be made a permanent policy, and I plead for something to be done on behalf of the apple crop in the maritime provinces. I say the maritime provinces because in New Brunswick we are going in extensively for the production of apples. Very fine orchards have been established along the Saint John river as well as in many other sections of the province, but unless something is done for this industry, which is very important to the maritimes, we shall have a serious time.
Another factor which operates very strongly against us is the freight rates. There is the Maritime Freight Rates Act, it is true. I shall not take time to debate that tonight, although I know that some members have said that we are not entitled to its benefits. But it was given to us many years ago and there is sound justification for continuing it. The railways are now proposing to increase their freight rates by thirty per cent. Hon. members will realize just what an increase of that size would mean to our farming and other industries in the maritime provinces.
There is another complaint which we had, and since the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) was allowed to discuss canned salmon, I think I can bring this matter up here. It has to do with our shipping industry. Considering the great difficulties which we have had in our provinces in the raising of our produce, potatoes and apples, and in the sale of them, we had expected that

Agricultural Products Act
they would be shipped, when they were shipped, from Canadian ports. But a few weeks ago shipments from western Canada, instead of going through either the port of Saint John or the port of Halifax, as our people had reason to believe they would, were diverted. Provision was made for these shipments to go through the port of Portland, Maine. Moreover, great quantities of potatoes which are being shipped from New Brunswick, and which have always been shipped from the port of Saint John, are to go through the port of Portland. Arrangements have been made to ship them through that port. That is a matter which the government should and must take into very careful consideration if they are to do justice to that part of Canada.
I am not going to discuss this matter further. We in the maritime provinces wish to do our share in providing food, not only for ourselves and for the rest of Canada, but also for Great Britain, but I suggest that this government should take into consideration the great handicaps under which we are trying to operate at the present time. We pay more for our farm machinery than any other part of Canada. We pay more in freight; we pay more for the fertilizer we use to produce our crops, more for our trucks, more for the feed we feed our dairy cattle and our hogs, and we are continually losing markets which we had in the past. The farmers of the maritimes are looking to this government to do something to enable them to operate on an equal footing with the farmers of other parts of the dominion.
We are going home tomorrow, most of us at any rate, and I should like to have a definite statement from the Minister of Agriculture. I feel that I and other members are entitled to know something definite which we can take back to our farmers, so that we can tell them what is being done, and that they may have at least some hope to enable them to carry on their very hard and difficult task.

Mr. Speaker, I had intended to offer the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) some gratuitious advice which I thought he would find valuable, and I still intend to do so before I get through, but I find it necessary, first, to reply to the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot). Because of the graciousness of his questions I think he is entitled to an answer. I only regret that time will not permit me to give him as complete an answer as I think he is entitled to.
First, I am going to make a recommendation to the hon. member for Temiscouata and other members on that side of the house from eastern Canada. It is that they might take a leaf from the book of the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol), who is extremely interested in irrigation and goes in his own time and
examines all irrigation schemes in Canada, looking into their possibilities, in order to make himself familiar with the subject. The result is that there is no better authority among the laymen in this house or in the country than the hon. member for Davenport.
He is a great man.

Yes. If some of my hon. friends on the other side would make the same kind of examination of conditions affecting the grain farmers of the west and their methods of marketing grain, much of the misunderstanding which it is evident the hon. member has would disappear, because many of the remarks he made could only have been made because of misinformation, since I know the hon. member is too honourable and honest to make these remarks without sincerely believing them to be true.
Briefly, I wish to point out to the hon. member that there are possibly three different kinds of concerns which own country elevators in the prairie provinces. There are over
5,000	of these elevators altogether. Some belong to the farmers themselves. In Alberta there is the Alberta wheat pool; in Saskatchewan, the Saskatchewan wheat pool, and in Manitoba, the Manitoba pool elevators. These are distinctly farmer-owned organizations. Then there is another kind called the united grain growers, which was at one time a farmer-owned organization, but some of whose shares have gradually, in the course of time, drifted into the hands of non-farmers, so that now it is partly farmer-owned and partly nonfarmer-owned. But it is a joint stock company.
The pools are co-operative in make-up. The united grain growers is a joint stock company, and there is the other kind, which are perfectly legitimate. They are owned either by private individuals or by private joint stock companies; they operate elevators for the purpose of taking in farmers' grain at a certain definite handling charge and commission for selling, and all operate the same way.
None of the pools at the present time pool grain as it was pooled before 1930. All operate in the same way. The farmer brings the grain in and it is purchased by the elevator agent. If it is wheat, at the present time, since September, 1943, the elevator company to which he goes takes it and makes the payment authorized by the wheat board for the particular type of wheat, issues a cash ticket, which is an advance payment, and a participation certificate which enables the farmer to share in any future payments the wheat board may make. The wheat board then controls the wheat and directs the elevator company, be it farmer-owned or partly farmer-owned
Agricultural Products Act

or completely privately owned, where to place the wheat so that the wheat board will have it in saleable position at all times.
I should like to go farther than that but time is not available. The minister gave a very good statement tonight, and an important one, when he said that the Winnipeg grain exchange has never been closed. The Winnipeg grain exchange is not an elevator company or a grain company. It is a market that has been established. It is obvious that no farmer can take a carload of grain and peddle it all over the world where grain can be sold, so that on the grain exchange the elevator company, or any individual who has a document that entitles him to a certain quantity of grain may, insofar as the grain exchange operates, go into their pit and offer that for sale. Buyers from all over the world, in the heyday of the business, would go to the pit and buy the grain, and that grain could then be sold at the prices agreed upon. That is the Winnipeg grain exchange, on which all elevator companies have seats which enable them to sell documents entitling them to ownership of grain. That is the purpose of the grain exchange. Whether this parliament or any law in the land has authority to close it, I do not know, but I do know that it could not exist if no grain were sold in that pit and commissions paid thereon.
I would ask the hon. member if he cares to do so, to listen carefully to the recommendations I am going to make to the minister as I go along. Before proceeding to that, however, I wish to join with the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) and the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) in their speeches this afternoon. With what they said I heartily agree. I will not repeat what they said because it is on the record in Hansard and it would be only taking up time to continue in that vein. They expressed opinions which many of us hold out there.
The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) dealt with some of the problems in grain handling and was questioned from this side of the house. Had I been asking the questions, my questions would have been different. I agree with the attitude he took that those people, both west of the prairie provinces and east of the prairies who are large buyers of our coarse grains, or of any of our grains, for feeding purposes should get those grains at prices they are able to pay and according to the kind of livestock feeding business they are in, and it is for that reason I wish to make certain recommendations to the minister tonight. I think they are recom-

mendations that can be supported by a very large body of opinion in western Canada; much larger, if I may say so, that those represented on the petition presented by the Searle Grain Company. Again I want to point out to the hon. member and any others who are interested that this petition, this letter to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon), accompanied by a letter from the Searle Grain Company and a letter from a farmer who is anonymous because there is no signature, does not deal with the matter of coarse grains which is under discussion here tonight. It is dealing entirely with the operations of the wheat board.
The Searle Grain Company have taken an attitude-and quite properly so if they feel like it; they have a perfect right to their ideas on the matter-entirely in opposition to what this group believe in, namely, the orderly marketing of wheat and what the government is doing at the present time under the British wheat contract. They are persistent and consistent in demanding that everything be done which would make it possible for open trading on the grain exchange which, as the minister has told us tonight, ceased to operate as far as wheat is concerned on September 23, 1943, I believe it was.
I believe there are one or two occasions in history when wheat trading on the Winnipeg exchange was suspended. I believe one was during the first world war in 1917 and 1918 and again in 1920; until the end of the crop year 1920; I think it was, when the old Canada wheat board was in operation. That is the position there, and I will return this letter to the hon. member, but it deals with wheat and with that opposition to the wheat marketing at the present time, and has nothing to do with the matter under discussion here tonight.
The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) this afternoon did express one or two ideas with which I think we could agree.
If my hon. friend will permit me to do so, I want to thank him for what he has just said and for the information he has just given.

The hon. member is welcome. I would give more if I had the time. I have plenty more here.
The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe made a statement, I think, that almost any fair-minded person in the house would have to agree with, namely, that if Canada is to make gifts or partial gifts to other countries, then all the taxpayers in Canada should share, in one form or another in the making

Agricultural Products Act
of that gift. While we agreed, and still agree, with the principle of long-term trading and bilateral trading if necessary-in fact, we see nothing wrong with the wheat contract with Britain!-we did hope and did express the hope when- we did agree with that in the initial stages, that this government would hold the price line with regard to the things the farmer has to buy. That was one of the things we emphasize and have emphasized continuously since that wheat board act. But that does not destroy our faith and belief in the act as a principle of marketing, even though we do not agree with the practical operation of it at the present time, in its entirety. So I agree with the hon. member for Dufferin^Simcoe in that and I agree with him in another statement-and I think every member of this house and everyone in this country would agree with this too-namely, that if we propose to sell wheat or eggs or fish or anything else that we have more of than we ourselves can consume, to another country, we must be prepared to take from that country an equal amount of goods which we need in this country and which we cannot produce ourselves or cannot produce as economically as they can. With regard to his remarks about the Minister of Agriculture-I do not know just what he called him; it was some kind of socialist, but not quite the same kind as I am, but both kinds he did not like-I do not agree with him there at all, and he would not expect me to.
The hon. member for Temiscouata also brought out another matter in connection with coarse grains. He wanted to know who was responsible for holding this grain up so that it did not get to the farmers whom he and others like him represent, in the agricultural communities or constituencies in the other parts of Canada. I do not know that I can lay the blame on any particular person. I think the blame is attributable to the kind of method we have used. I believe the Minister of Agriculture and the government made a very serious error when they did not do one of two things, namely, either announce the increase in the price of coarse grains at the start of the new grain season, which is on August 1 of every year, or else at that time have placed it completely under the operations of the wheat board, so that whatever changes took place in the price at a later date would be reflected back in>
wheat board payments to deliveries of coarse grain. One of those two methods should have been followed. Neither of them was.
The result was that the elevator companies accepted the coarse grain, paid for it at the price as it was according to the grain exchange
price, either between the floor or the ceiling price as explained by the Minister of Agriculture, and then sold that grain. No elevator company holds the grain. If my hon. friend will read the Sir Josiah Stamp report, it said that those who finance the elevator companies will not allow them to hold grain on borrowed money, that is, money borrowed from the banks. Most of them do borrow from banks. I do not know any that do not, unless possibly Searle; but I do not know of any others. Therefore, by their agreement with their banks, when they borrow they immediately sell that grain, deducting therefrom their spreads, freight and other costs and get it into a position where it is deliverable against a contract. When it gets to that place, somebody else has it.
So far as a pool official ever recommending that the farmers hold that grain and speculate in it, I very much doubt that statement and I think the hon. member has been misinformed there, because, while something that may appear like that may have happened, that would not be it. Remember that I mentioned that the wheat board took it. Remember that the wheat board, once the wheat is delivered, have the right to order that wheat to whatever position they require it for sales. Remember that navigation closes on the great lakes. Therefore the wheat must be moved to tide water as rapidly as possible, particularly if it is coming east, before navigation closes. Obviously the wheat board wants that grain to go down the lakes then. Therefore it must be loaded into cars, brought to the terminals, loaded in the ships and unloaded, and stored down here where it can go out by ocean-going freight during the winter season, because the rail haul is very long from Port Arthur down to our Atlantic ocean ports. Some goes to the western ports, it is true.
It is true that the wheat board did ask the elevator companies to use every available car that they could, commensurate with the space in their elevators, to move the wheat forward as fast as possible. It is quite possible-I do not know this; the Minister of Trade and Commerce could answer this better than I- that the wheat board did ask the terminal elevators to load boats with wheat as rapidly as possible before navigation closed. But I do know that this year was a normal one so far as movement of coarse grains are concerned from the farms down to the terminals. Usually, wheat being the big cash group, the farmers will move more wheat or a larger amount of wheat in the fall than they will coarse grain. There are some farmers who
Agricultural Products Act

raise more coarse grain as their cash crop than wheat and they obviously sell theirs. The result is that the normal movement of coarse grain during the fall months will run between forty or sixty per cent of the coarse grain supply for market in any one year. This year I understand it ran about sixty per cent, which would be right at the top level of normal. Therefore the farmer did not hold it. I have explained that the elevator companies would bring it down and place it in the contract position. Who buys it then and what they do with it, of course is their business and nobody can say whether they do rightly or wrongly. As long as it is private business, they have a perfect right to hold it and they have a perfect right to do what they like with it. Whether they held it or not, I could not say.

Will the hon.
member permit a question?
Yes.

Do you know that until about a week ago the wheat board forbade the all-rail movement of coarse grain from western Canada to the east? Until just about one week ago that was forbidden, which was, of course, the reason there was no competition.

To a large extent the hon. member is correct. I am not going to argue about that. The wheat board had probably sound ideas for doing that. I hardly think it is quite as bad as that. However, that is not the whole story. There are other people who enter into it. I am not going to criticize them. It is the policy I am criticizing. I am simply trying to point out the things that happened. What the hon. member for Calgary West says may be perfectly true but there were other responsible individuals. I am not going to hold them guilty; I will say "responsible".
I have here a little paper printed at Cowans-ville, in the province of Quebec. It is called "The Church, Farm and Town", and the editor is Reverend John Peacock. He states that the farmers of that district held meetings, which were quite well attended, protesting against the increase in the price of feed grains. He gives two stories; the second one, which I am going to quote, may point to those who, to some extent, were responsible for holding up grain. He says:
The second story is of a lake boat filled with grain-
That is coarse grains.

left at a dockside (Toronto, I think it was) for from ten days to two weeks with no attempt

being made to unload and ship it to the market, until the day of the removal of the subsidy, and the subsequent price rise.
That is the story printed in this paper, and I suppose some things like that happened. They could not have happened if what I am now going to recommend to the minister and the government had been done; that is the same thing the hon. member for New Westminster just asked the minister. I know the minister will not agree to the suggestion now, but I wish he would say here the things I have heard him say at meetings in the country. I always attend any meeting in the country at which the minister is present, if I can possibly do so; when he spoke in the Elks Hall in our city on October 10 of this year I cancelled what to me were important engagements in order to listen to him, because he is always interesting and informative; and, besides, it is just as well to keep as close track of him as possible when he is in Saskatchewan. At that meeting the minister was discussing the wheat marketing policy and various points of view. During the course of that discussion, he said the private grain trade, the private elevator companies and others did not agree with the present method of marketing wheat. He went on to say, quite rightly, I think, that they had a perfect right to that opinion, but he stated that the organized farmers did agree that this was the right principle, and he added, "I agree, and I take my advice from the organized farmers." That indicated clearly that the minister is an intelligent man. It also indicated that he is learning that the organized farmers know what they want and why they want it. It also indicated that the government believes it worth while to listen to people who get together to present their own points of view and suggest different methods.
I have no quarrel with the minister up to that point, but I want to point out to him, if he meant what he said on that occasion, that he would prefer to take his advice from the organized farmers, that at three successive annual meetings of the Saskatchewan wheat pool resolutions were passed asking that oats and barley as well as flaxseed be included in the operations of the wheat board. So, if the minister prefers the opinion and advice of the organized farmers he should not disregard their advice concerning the marketing of coarse grain, any more than he should disregard it in connection with the marketing of wheat. Of course the minister may say the government has not power to do this. On more than one occasion in this house I have been twitted because of my lack of legal knowledge. I humbly confess I have very

Agricultural Products Act
little legal knowledge. When my little operations are against the law I carry them on where there is no law to watch me, so that I do not need a lawyer to help me; and I never have operations big enough, and never have any intention to break the law, so that I do not have to hire a lawyer to find a loophole for me. But I do understand English when it is put in the ordinary way, and I want to point out that subsection 2 of section 7 of the act amending the Canadian Wheat Board Act, which we considered last session, states:
Except as directed by the governor in council, the board shall not buy grain, other than wheat.
If a law is passed saying that, except by a certain order of the governor in council, which I believe is the cabinet, you must not do something, it must automatically follow that if the order is passed you can do that thing; otherwise there is no meaning to the phrase. I would ask any lawyer here if I am wrong in my interpretation. If, under certain conditions, a certain body in authority may allow you to do a certain thing, is it not implied that the power to do it is there, once the authority is given by that body? So for the life of me I do not see how the minister can say the government does not have authority. When he speaks I hope he will clear up this point, though he is not a lawyer, either. He used to be a schoolteacher, however, and should be able to put it into words even I can understand, without the need for any legal phraseology.
Not only did the minister say at a public meeting in my hearing that he preferred to take the advice of organized farmers. I want him to tell me if I am to believe press reports of a meeting which I did not attend but which was addressed by the minister and also by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), who is the leader of the Liberal party in Saskatchewan. Both these gentlemen are reported to have said at that Liberal caucus or public meeting in Saskatchewan that they believed coarse grains should be included in the operations of the wheat board and that they would press for their inclusion at the next session of parliament, meaning this very session. When the minister speaks tonight I hope he will do that very thing and make the initial move to have this done, as well as explain why the government has not the legal power in spite of the paragraph I read.
Someone may ask why I am requesting that coarse grains be included in the operations of the wheat board.

I shall go on with what I was going to recommend. I pointed out a while ago-and I tried to be careful to lay no blame on anybody, either the elevator companies, or the grain exchange or those who process or handle the feed here-that the farmers in eastern Canada, and I know the farmers on the prairies and in all parts of Canada where they sell their grain are, with few exceptions, disappointed in the policy.
I believe it could be made agreeable to all concerned by an act of this House of Commons, if necessary, and by enabling legislation from the provinces, if that is necessary, which would meet the very suggestion mentioned by the hon. member for Temiscouata, namely, the need for co-ordination of interest, among the various farmers of Canada. And because of that, I believe it would be proper for the government here to include coarse grains in the operations of the wheat board now, or as quickly as possible.
I believe it would be proper to make a survey, because the livestock industry is in a serious condition in, this country. It would be proper to make a survey of the livestock population and the amount of feed available, to see if that amount of feed, will carry the necessary livestock through the necessary period of time, either as breeding or as marketable stock, until it comes to that position.
I believe they should then, through the wheat board, if it has control of coarse grains, make those feeding supplies available where and as required, either at prices the feeders can pay and at prices the grower can afford to sell them, or, if that cannot be done, by subsidy, to either or both, so as to make that possible.
I believe that it is an expedient. I know it is an expedient; it is not a long-term policy. I would not want to see it carried out forever in this country, but it could be carried out until such time as production catches up so as to make it possible for the livestock producer and the coarse grain producer to act with some degree of assurance. With that survey, and with the wheat board handling coarse grain, I believe then that the things suggested by the hon. member for Temiscouata can be done, because I know there is widespread discontent all across Canada.
Then,, for the government to be fair with all concerned, because the price increase was not announced until October 22-I believe that was the date-some provision would have

to be made. There were quite a number of farmers who did deliver coarse grains at lower prices. There were some, of course, who for various reasons did not. Mr. Speaker, one purpose of my rising at this time is to fulfil a promise which I made shortly before I came here to a very angry gathering of farmers. Like the hon. member for New
Agricultural Products Act

Westminster (Mr. Reid), I attended a gathering that had been called by the federation of agriculture. It is needless for me to go into the details of that meeting because the story is well known. We heard the story of the liquidation of breeding stock, the slaughtering of young pigs, the killing of laying pullets and the drying up of dairy cattle. The farmers at that meeting were indignant at the policies which had been pursued by this government and, in my opinion, those policies were the direct result of the Agricultural Products Act which we are supposed to be debating.
I wish to say that, while considerable indignation was expressed at that meeting there was no suggestion that the government had done wrong in lifting the price ceilings on coarse grains. The farmers in my part of the country are quite willing to see the farmers in western Canada get all they can for their coarse grain. They felt that the western farmers were entitled to it, but what they were particularly displeased about was the timing and the fact that prices were still held down on the products of the eastern farmer who consumes those coarse grains.
When this act was going through the house last spring this party opposed it. I gave as my reason for opposing it that I considered it to be pure socialism. I took the stand that the more of these socialistic policies we adopted, the harder it would be to get away from them. I took the stand also that I considered it most unjust and most unfair to give the government power to control and regulate and generally mess around with farm prices when no control was exercised over farm costs. I was sure then, and I am more than ever convinced now, that a policy of that kind would lead only to disaster.
Of course this act is only part of the government's much touted and supposedly beautiful plan of orderly control. I never did like the idea of orderly decontrol because I think it is a vicious principle. It was a catch phrase to lull the people into thinking that everything was being carried along in a smooth and well conceived way, whereas in reality it has been a policy of fumbling, floundering and inexpediency. In my opinion it is unjust, unsound and unworkable.
It was all very well for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) to say the other day that the farmers were chronic kickers, that they were getting more now than they had ever got before. It is perfectly true that the farmers are getting higher prices than they got in 1939, but it must be remembered that in 1939 farm prices were lower than they had been before the first war and that costs were at least

seventy-five per cent higher than they were at that time. That ratio has persisted or has even increased since that time. That is something which many people do not take into consideration when they talk about farmers being chronic kickers. They may be, but it may also be that they have something to kick about.
Last spring the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) intimated that he realized that the farmers were not getting a fair deal. It was all very well for him to say that, while they were not getting a fair break, still they did not need the money that other people needed. They wore old clothes and old boots, they did1 not dress up and so it did not matter so much.
I did not say that. If the hon. member is just adding that on, that is all right.
I would not say that those are the exact words, but that was the implication.
I am a farmer and I dress just as well as the hon. member.

If hon. members will look up page 1496 of Hansard of March 18, 1947, I think they will find that I come quite near to quoting the minister correctly. That may be all quite true; but what the average farmer of this country, and especially the young farmer, is becoming more and more rebellious about is the fact that he is compelled to work so many hours that he does not have a chance to put on his good clothes, that he has not a chance to enjoy the leisure and amenities enjoyed by the average working man in town who quite often works only a forty-hour week. In my opinion the working man in town does not give the same service to society as the average farmer does.
Last spring the government asked parliament to give them the powers contained in this bill so that they could stabilize agricultural conditions. I do not for one moment question the good intention or the honesty of purpose of the government and its advisers in doing what they thought was the proper thing to do, but, while they are very able and wise men, they are not endowed with the powers of divinity and they should not attempt to assume those powers to perform miracles.
The stabilization of agriculture is a myth and must necessarily be so, because no one could possibly foresee that conditions in Europe could be as terrible as they are. I submit that that is the very point. Even in normal times the world is never static, and

Agricultural Products Act
no one can foretell what will happen, even within the next few hours. So that to try to create 'better conditions by price fixing and control and fumbling around is futile. I do not need to go into any more details, because the ground has been well covered from all angles by much abler speakers than I. I close by intimating, if it has not already been guessed, that I do not like this legislation and am definitely opposed to it.

Mr. Speaker, I am afraid I shall find it difficult to restrain myself to the extent my hon. friend the member for Swift Current (Mr. Bentley) did in discussing the question before us, which is of such vital concern to us farmers who have been so closely connected with farm work and farm organizations as my colleague and I have been. Although we are all anxious to conclude the work before us in time to get home and be with our families for Christmas, I cannot let this opportunity pass without adding my voice of protest against some of the things that have gone on; and, as I said before, I might find it difficult to restrain myself to the extent my colleague did.
Yet what can we do about the matter? The resolution before us, first of all, asks for an extension of this measure for a period of three months only, which, in my opinion, is insufficient to be of any great use, and I shall deal with that a little later. Second, what have the government, and especially the Department of Agriculture, done with the powers granted to them in the past? More important still, what do they indend to do with these powers in the future? The Biblical phrase is quite applicable to this situation: "Give an account of thy stewardship: for thou mayest be no longer steward."
I wish to deal for a moment with the three months' extension asked for. All hon. members know that, had parliament not been summoned at this time, the act would have remained in operation until March 31 next. No one knows better than the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) that the farmers of this country need a period of that many years, rather than months, in which to plan their operations properly. But parliament was called together, not in the early part of November as it should have been, but on a date that left us no time to do any of the things that should be attended to, and we are placed in the position of having to put our stamp of approval on this half-baked proposal.
What has been done during these past two weeks? Nothing except to extend the emergency powers act, which was in the same
category as this resolution inasmuch as it would have continued in effect until March 31 next had parliament not been summoned at this time. All the other questions have been laid on the shelf until parliament meets early or late in the new year. In my humble opinion, there was no valid excuse for not summoning parliament earlier. If that had been done we could have given proper attention to all these matters.
I do not want to be unfair when I say that nothing has been done during the past two weeks, because the government have done something. They have flown a number of kites in an attempt to find out in which direction the political winds are blowing. I might go so far as to say that they have sent aloft an observation balloon in the hope of finding out what the temperature of the farmers is since the government adopted its present policies. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers' temperature is pretty high; in other words, it is hot. I can perhaps best give their reaction to the government's policy by quoting what the Hon. I. C. Nollett, of the Saskatchewan government, said. These were his words:
I have never seen the farmers so hopping mad as they were when the price ceilings and subsidies were removed from oats and barley.
I should also Like to read a letter from one of my constituents, one of dozens and dozens of letters, and the same view has been expressed by hundreds of farmers who have approached me, all protesting against this action of the government.
They must be a lot of grumblers.
If the hon. member for Renfrew North (Mr. Warren) would hold his peace for a moment he might learn something. This letter is dated November 9, and addressed to myself.
Western grumblers.

It reads:
Dear Sir:
I understand that a session of parliament will soon open and you probably will have a chance to make known at Ottawa the feelings and problems of your electors. I have therefore taken this opportunity to let you know how many of the farmers in your constituency feel about the lifting of price control on oats and barley. First of all, I must mention that even people who have no livestock feel that the throwing of barley and oats on the grain exchange was a very inappropriate move.
As far as livestock producers are concerned, it is still worse as, with the price of barley and oats at the present level, it is impossible to raise pigs, dairy cattle and poultry on a profitable basis. I am mainly concerned with swine

production and will therefore confine my next remarks on that line, being more familiar with it.
This year and for the last ten years, I have marketed on the average over 200 pigs a year. At times our profit was not very large but never have we had as bad a blow as we had this last time. As it is now, I have thirty brood sows on hand, many of A. (R. breeding, but by the 1st of January, if nothing is done to encourage bacon production, I shall take the only course left open; ship them to the packing plants. And I will not be the only one as already many sows are seen in the stock yards in . . .
Under present arrangements we are buying feed on which there is no ceiling but selling our pork under one. I have had many years practical experience raising pigs and have graduated with the bachelor of agriculture, specialized in animal husbandry from the University of Saskatchewan but I must admit that I still cannot buy barley at $1.10, pay hauling charge, hire labour at $80 a month and feed that barley to pigs on a profitable basis.
If this policy is continued much longer into the breeding season there will not be a pound of pork to be bought in western Canada next summer. I would therefore appreciate it if you would put up a fight on this subject at the coming session as your constitutency is hard hit by this policy, having much livestock.
This is only one of hundreds of people who have protested to me about this situation. In that connection, sir, I wish to draw to your attention the fact that, even as this man mentions, those who are not concerned with the production or feeding of livestock are vitally interested and are anxious about the situation, because they see something that has been built up over past years, something that has been encouraged by this very government, being broken down. They see something that has been built up being destroyed, and they know that this added cost going into the production of livestock, dairy and poultry products will affect them sooner or later, because it will enter into increased costs of these products, making it impossible for many people to buy them. And so we have once more the vicious spiral of prices. That is what these men see, even those who are not producing livestock, and it is something that I would impress upon some members who have spoken before, both in and out of the house, accusing western farmers of not having delivered their feed grains.
The question asked by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) has been very well answered by my colleague and deskmate, but there are others who ask similar questions, and I want them to know that the farmers continued to deliver their feed grain in the normal manner of other years, in spite of the fact that in many sections of

the province from which I come there was an almost total failure in the line of feed grains.
There are large areas in that province and in my own neighbourhood where in past years we have always produced heavily in coarse grains, and it was almost a failure. From my own farm where I used to deliver 100 bushels of feed grain in years gone by I oould deliver only one bushel this year. I had only one bushel of feed grain for every 100 bushels I used to deliver years ago, and even those few bushels were delivered in the normal course of time, notwithstanding wdiat some hon. members have tried to make out.
Something was said about the re-opening of the Winnipeg grain exchange. The minister put some of these people right in their thinking. In fact I do not know where they were last session or some of the sessions preceding that one, because the minister has explained the situation on a number of occasions just as ably as he has explained it tonight. But the minister and my colleague and deskmate, the hon. member for Swift Current, could have gone a little farther with respect to the Winnipeg grain exchange. What my desk-mate said is quite true. We have somebody else to do the selling for us and we pay that person a commission for it. What I should have liked the minister to explain further is that the beneficial part of the grain exchange has so far disappeared; that to all intents and purposes it has outlived its usefulness, because some people have gone and abused the privileges of the exchange to such an extent that it is a regular gambler's dive.
Every once in a while it comes to my attention that branches of the Canadian Legion, charitable organizations, service clubs and so on are notified that games of chance, including bingo, are contrary to the criminal code of Canada. I could never understand why those in charge of our legislation and our government should be so solicitous about protecting us from bingo. I would say this to the

Why not handle grain through the pools?

The farmers, not only of my constituency but throughout the west, were riled, and during the latter part of the fall the people in my constituency had the idea that they would now be in a position where they would have the matter explained to them, because there appeared posters on the billboards, advertisements in the local paper, advertising under the auspices of the Humboldt Liberal federal executive, of a public meeting to be addressed by the Right Hon. James G. Gardiner, Minister of Agriculture. That advertising went on for a couple of weeks. Then the night of the meeting came. The hall was in darkness. The people had come in from a considerable distance; and, as far as I could find out, no attempt had been made to notify the people that the meeting had been cancelled. Mind you, Mr. Speaker, some of the farmers who drove in thirty miles to hear the Minister of Agriculture telephoned to the secretary of the C.C.F. to ask why the Minister of Agriculture was not speaking.
What co-operation!

That was a disappointment. Quite frankly I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that, had the minister appeared, I would have gone to the meeting, just like my colleague and deskmate apparently did in Swift Current. But while that was bad enough, something happened a few weeks later that was a good deal worse.
It is not so bad as to have had to listen.

You would have a big crowd that night, would you not?

The advertisements kept on going, and all at once I said to some of my friends, "What is going on?" because I had just heard on the radio that the hon. member for Rosthern and another gentleman were on their way to Ottawa. Well, my friends did not know. Even that afternoon someone put a general ring over the rural telephone lines- and we have over 500 rural subscribers connected with our central-
And they all listen in.

-urging the farmers to come in and hear the hon. member for Rosthern discuss the coarse grain situation, when they certainly knew that the hon. member for Rosthern was so far up in the air that he would not be able to discuss anything with anybody in Humboldt. Mr. Speaker-

speechtext: I would ask that the hon. member be asked to withdraw that remark.
