speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It may have been dishonest to go down and work for the farmers.

If in the course of my remarks I might have left the inference that I believed that the hon. member for Rosthern was responsible for the advertising and that, therefore, I was accusing him, I wish to assure him that was farthest from my mind, because I certainly know enough about this little political game to know he would not have been doing the advertising. But I do know this much. It was common knowledge that he and his associate were in Ottawa at the time that the general ring was being put over the rural line at Humboldt; and I still contend that whoever was responsible was playing dishonest politics when he encouraged people to come in and hear the hon. member for Rosthern discuss the feed grain situation, when he knew the hon. member for Rosthern could not be there.
To get this whole thing straight now, Mr. Speaker-and I am serious about it, because I do not like to have my people disappointed and fooled around with like that-I wish to extend an invitation here tonight to the Minister of Agriculture, the hon. member for Rosthern, and-if he would consent to come and if the hon. member for Rosthern would not object too much-to the leader of the opposition-
How about the hon, member for Humboldt? He ought to be there.

-to come to Humboldt at any given time during this Christmas recess; and if they give me time enough, I will organize a meeting and let them explain the feed grain situation to the people in that constituency. All that I will ask, Mr. Speaker, besides having the honour and privilege of introducing the gentlemen, is that I have fifteen minutes at the end of the time.
Send me an invitation. I will take another five minutes after you.

There is one thing I wanted to say. In spite of all the assertions made by the hon. member for Rosthern that I was

Agricultural Products Act
getting considerable assistance from our Tory friends, I wish to say that in so far as trying to put the hon. member and members on the government side right in their thinking as to what the farmers of this country think, I do not care where the help comes from; we are going to tell them that the farmers of this country want a different kind of deal than the one they have been getting. I enjoy the interjections that have been made, although sometimes it was difficult to know whether I or the hon. member for Rosthern or the hon. member for Waterloo was making the speech.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: You think you need help from the Conservatives, do you?

Why did you not go to
Prince Edward Island?
Where have you been?

Like my colleague the hon. member for Swift Current, I have a number of suggestions, or I might call them questions, with which I should like the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to deal when he takes part in this debate. Some of them may have been touched upon already; nevertheless they are of such vital concern to our farmers that I shall proceed with them as I have them listed here.
1.	Is the government going to have the meat board see to it that packing plants and others will not have an opportunity to cash in on the forced liquidation of our livestock?
2.	Will those farmers who sold their grain prior to the lifting of the ceilings be reimbursed for their losses?
3.	Will the government reconsider action by way of subsidies or other assistance in the feeding of livestock, hogs, etc.?
4.	Does the government intend to continue discouraging the livestock industry in the prairie provinces, thereby nullifying all the good work done in this respect during the past few years?
As I said, I would appreciate being able to take back to the people I have the honour to represent a clear-cut statement by the minister as to what may be expected, not only by the farmers of my constituency, but by the farmers of eastern, central and western Canada, in reference to the livestock program.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I convey to you and to all hon. members of this house my sincere yuletide greetings. May I also add that when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) spoke yesterday, and, I believe, on other occasions, he referred to the forces of evil that have been unleashed in some parts of the world. I would be among the first to acknowledge that we are facing one of the most critical periods the civilized world has 5849-31}
ever known, but in my humble opinion much of the trouble is caused by the fact that so many people in our so-called Christian nations have forgotten or refused to follow the lessons taught by the Prince of Peace. If only we would endeavour to establish within ourselves and, then, within the circle and community in which we move and live the spirit of the brotherhood of man under the common fatherhood of God, and place at the feet of the Babe of Bethlehem as our Christmas offering, I am sure our future Christmases would be happy and our New Years bright.

Mr. Speaker, I am surprised at myself in rising to take part in this debate this evening. I made up my mind to do so only a very short time ago, and then because of a name which has been often mentioned and which, I assume, is regarded as one of the forces of evil just referred to by the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Burton). I refer to the Winnipeg grain exchange, about which I intend to have something to say before I conclude.
Before doing so, I should like to direct the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to this evening's Ottawa Journal, which carries a dispatch from Melbourne under the heading, "Britain paying S2.72 for wheat from Australia". The dispatch goes on to say that India is buying wheat from Australia at S2.96, and both these prices are f.o.b. Australia, while the United States is selling wheat at S3. I would call to the minister's attention also the last quotation I was able to get, which shows a comparison between the quality of Canadian No. 1 wheat and Australian No. 1 wheat in Liverool. The quotation is for April, 1938, and covers the sale of wheat in six-bushel lots. The price for Canadian No. 1 was 51 shillings; for Australian No. 1, 34 shillings, or a difference of 17 shillings in a six-bushel lot. This means a differential of 56 cents a bushel as between the two wheats at that time, while today our wheat of higher quality is being sold to Britain at SI .55 as against S2.72 being obtained by Australia. I mention that, saying nothing more about it, only in order to express the hope that when the minister takes part in this debate he will give some explanation as to the difference in position between ourselves and our neighbouring commonwealth.
A moment ago I stated that I intended to say something about the marketing of wheat and, without camouflaging it, something about
the Winnipeg grain exchange. I remember that last year I had something to say on a matter affecting the railways, and I told the house-I believe it is a sound practice-that what I said would have to be accepted with
4S4
Agricultural Products Act

whatever you cared to take away from it because on occasion I had acted for both our railway companies. In this connection, however, I immediately absolve myself of any connection. I do not act for the Winnipeg grain exchange; I have never done so. I do not act, and for at least fifteen years have not acted, for any elevator company or anyone connected with the grain business. So that in what I say I do not believe I can be successfully accused of any self-interest.
Everyone who has referred to this institution in Winnipeg, including three hon. members tonight, has used the word "gambling." They are greatly horrified. We are told that bingo was prohibited in schoolhouses; yet this den of iniquity, as I think it was called, or this gambling dive, was allowed to operate. So let us have a word or two about gambling. If I want to gamble in anything there are always plenty of places where I can do so and plenty of persons who will copper my bets, unless my bets are so out of line that they should not be covered. If I want to gamble I can go to Toronto the good, as I believe it is called, where they have a stock exchange. Will anyone suggest to me for a moment that a person who buys nickel and dime stocks is buying them for investment? The suggestion is silly. We buy cheap stock on various exchanges in the hope that there will be a rise in the price of those stocks. Investment has long since ceased to be a factor except in established stocks, bonds, preferred shares and things of that kind. So in Chicago-I am not considering the matter of exchange control- we had open all during the war, and all during the first war, a grain exchange. In later years we had the exchange at Kansas City, and until recently the Liverpool exchange. So if someone merely wishes to gamble in grain, the Winnipeg grain exchange is of no particular importance, because we can do all the so-called gambling we like in Chicago. What is the set-up with respect to the marketing of grain, and what is the set-up of the Winnipeg grain exchange? I greatly fear-and I speak respectfully of those people who have been using extravagant language in their attacks upon this institution-that, frankly, they do not know what they are talking about. I do not say that in any spirit of vengefulness or in any desire to be unkind. I say it because I mean just what I say.
What is the situation with respect to the marketing of wheat and coarse grains, or let us say, grains grown in the west, because they are practically the only ones dealt with on that exchange? We have many grain growers. We have many elevator companies, and we

have a pool in each of the provinces. We have also a co-operative company called the united grain growers, which certainly operates in Alberta and in Saskatchewan, although I do not think they are in Manitoba. I am not sure about that-I imagine they must be, because the Hon. Mr. Crerar is one of the persons who began that company. It is a co-operative show.
What happens? These elevator companies are not the Winnipeg grain exchange. They are elevator companies dealing in the purchase and. sale of grain. The Winnipeg grain exchange is an entirely separate body, where persons may buy and sell without going into the country, and without even owning a single elevator.
What happens? Let us assume I am a farmer and in the fall of the year I have 1,000 bushelis of wheat. I intend to speak about the glut in the elevators, because that is the word used, although, as I believe I shall demonstrate before I shall have finished, there is no justification for it. But let us say I have 1,000 bushels of wheat. I draw it to the elevator nearest my farm and can do two things with it. I can sell it and get cash tickets for it, or I can leave it there and get storage tickets for it. If I sell it, it belongs to whoever bought it. If I get storage tickets, it is mine.
It is perfectly true it will be mixed, because it is a small lot. It will be mixed with other grain, shipped east and graded. However, I rvill be paid the grade on the day I bring it there, given to me by the man who grades it and buys it.
We will say that is in October. I, the farmer, think the price is too low. What do I do? I buy a December or May option; I do not know whether December is open or not. However, I buy a futures option, because I think that grain is too cheap at the price at whidh I sold it. Is that gambling? Well, if it is gambling, then the farmers of this country are doing as much as or more gambling than any other people.

Has the hon. member any idea of what percentage of farmers use that facility, or what percentage of trading on the Winnipeg grain exchange is carried on by genuine farmers? I would say it was less than one per cent.
Any farmer thinks he can make a profit.
Perhaps I might be allowed to answer, if I may.
We are pretty fortunate to have an authority with this information.
Agricultural Products Act
Which authority is that?
You are the authority we are listening to.

I do not speak to you as an authority. I speak to you as a teacher of the lower grades, hoping that you will ultimately absorb the principles of what I am talking about.
May I say this, that I know many farmers of my personal acquaintance who do exactly that. And may I say this, too, that it is wide open for anyone to do it.
I have been in the house for four sessions, and this grain exchange has been kicked around, abused, and rough language used in respect of it every year I have been here. As I say, I have no interest in it, but they have nobody to speak for them; and I intend, if I can, to put both sides of the picture before the bouse. If anybody wishes to ask any direct questions when I have finished, I shall give equally direct answers. There will not be any evasion so far as I am concerned. It will be remembered that I have a tremendous farming community in my constituency and I know I am not doing myself, personally, much good. But I think time will prove it will do me good.
The farmer takes this 1,000 bushels and sells it at a dollar, to use round figures. He buys in his option, and when the time comes- and he may 'have held his grain and paid storage on it, and insurance-he then can deliver the grain against that option. He must do that, or he must settle on the date. Supposing the price has gone down. He must settle, and the usual way he does it is to switch-that is the word they use-his purchase to the next settlement date, which will probably be the July date. Does anybody see anything very wrong with that? Certainly I do not.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: If this man has bought wheat in August and put up a certain amount of margin, and then someone with sufficient money comes along and puts up a sufficiently large margin, can he not sell enough wheat short to drive that price down and perhaps close out the person who has bought wheat in the manner suggested by the hon. member?

The only answer I can make to that is that that particular question has been asked of every grain commission set up in Canada, two of which were conducted by Mr. Justice Turgeon, one of the ablest men you and I know, and at the present time our ambassador to Eire. He found on every occasion that a short interest-and that is what you are talking about-was beneficial to the producers of grain in the Dominion of Canada. That was the finding of Mr. Justice Turgeon on two distinct occasions.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I do not remember that finding. Is it not true that a short interest like that drives the price down? Does the hon. member not admit that if a man has enough money to put up a sufficiently large margin he can sell grain that does not exist at all, and drive the price down.
Why don't you sell that policy to your party?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: That is the policy of our party in Saskatchewan.
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Is this the policy of the Progressive Conservative party then, that the hon. member is putting forward? That is not the way they talk in Saskatchewan.
Leave it to Smith; he will answer that.
I gather that . you are through with your questions and your abuse and your nonsense, I hope.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: There is no nonsense about it. You said you would give a direct answer. And when you say my question is nonsense, that is not correct.

I repeat that your question was the worst kind of nonsense. Let us have no argument about it. You know perfectly well, if you know anything about this business at all, that wheat has been cornered only once in this world, and that was by a Canadian who came from Guelph, and who was then resident in Chicago.
And who died broke.

You can go through all those investigations, and the hardest thing a commission can do is to set out to find a professional short seller. The Turgeon commission did not find one in the whole city of Winnipeg. That is one of the things which ought to be put straight.
May I apologize to the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) for being a little short myself. It does not do either of us any good to lose our tempers. I am afraid I lost mine, and he is too nice a fellow to quarrel with anyway.
We come down now to the exchange itself, and its membership. Who are the members?
Agricultural Products Act

Every pool in western Canada-the Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba pools; they are the members. They used the facilities of the grain exchange up until the very day when the wheat board took over the compulsory marketing of grain. I am sure the Minister of Agriculture will agree with me in that.
They are some of the members.

The three
pools were all members. Let me go a step farther. The three pools all had members on the executive which controlled the exchange, and I imagine they still have. I know they had prior to the time the wheat board took over the general marketing. That is the sort of structure that this terrible thing is.
May I immediately admit, on the other hand, that there were people who had no wheat who came in and played the wheat market. I did so myself. I took my only trip to England in 1928. I had SI,000 and I promised my wife that we would go. I went to a grain broker there and I said, "Is wheat a sell or a buy?" That is how much I knew about the matter. He said, "Look out the window; this is Friday; if it rains by Monday, it is a sell; if it does not, it is a buy." I looked at the sky-that was in May and I was sailing in June-and I thought that it would never rain. So I put up my $1,000 as margin. Over the week end the biggest rain we had ever had started and it was still raining on Monday morning. I telephoned to have them sell me out and I lost my $1,000 and I owed them $1.65. That was my one transaction in trying to play the wheat market and the Winnipeg grain exchange. I am not complaining because I got what I asked for. I had a run for my money, but the rain had the biggest run.
The Winnipeg grain exchange is controlled by this executive. Let us take 1,000 bushels and see what happens. The farmer sells the 1,000 bushels to the elevator company. What does the elevator company do with them? We will say the elevator pays the farmer cash for his wheat. It then goes from the possession of the farmer and is the property of the elevator company. As everyone who knows anything about the business knows, every country elevator reports daily ithe bushelage which it has bought that day, and then it sells the grain at the opening of the market the following day. The idea that the elevator companies are gambling on the markets is pure nonsense. A couple of them tried it and went broke, and some of their managers are still in the penitentiary.

There is no truth in the accusation that the elevator companies are gambling with the farmers' wheat. They do not do that. They make their money from handling charges and by having grain in position to take care of markets. It may be that there is a two-cent premium at Vancouver or something like that, which happens quite often, and they would have the grain in what they call position to be able to get it quickly to such a market.
We all received copies of the resolution passed by the Alberta farmers' union which threatened that, unless the grain exchange was closed, they would put on a farmers' strike in Alberta in the next grain season. That has been in all 'the papers and I assume it is public property. I do not think any of us here believe that legislation of that kind will come through coercion or threat by any organization, be it in my own province or be it anywhere else. If that be so, we are not much of a parliament.
We talk about closing the exchange. The Minister of Agriculture can tell us that the exchange has never been closed. Of course it has never been closed. How are you going to close it? In effect, the dominion government can close it by compulsorily taking all the grain. They would then have nothing left to trade with. They might still be open, but for all practical purposes they would be closed. As I say, you cannot be in the clothes-pin business unless you have some clothes-pins to buy and sell. It is the same with grain; you must have something to trade.
What could we do by way of legislation? Let us assume that we passed an act closing the Winnipeg grain exchange. I think there would be plenty of trouble with the Manitoba government because they would say immediately that we were going beyond our jurisdiction. That is something which you just cannot do. What else could we do? I am glad the minister who was recently Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) is in the chamber. In my humble opinion, the only way it could be done would be to add something to the criminal code similar to what we have to deal with gambling houses and that sort of thing. By statute we could make trading in grain a criminal offence, because we have the power to do that. But certainly that would be stretching things a terribly long way. It would be doing indirectly what we have no right to do directly.
In my time-let that cover at least fifty years-the Winnipeg grain exchange has been closed twice. On both occasions it was closed on a rising market, and the farmers of western Canada paid the price of those two closings

Agricultural Products Act
because they had government boards and did not get the price to which grain rose in the world market. Those are the only two occasions on which this den of iniquity has been closed or put out of business by its commodity being taken away from it.
Let us get right down to the question, because I do not want anyone to have any doubt as to where I stand. Of course I am speaking personally, as I have been throughout this evening. I might be asked: Are you in favour of the operation of the grain exchange? I am going to answer the question by saying, first, that I do not know the men who operate it. However, I think I shall satisfy everybody when I say that I am in favour of the farmer having an opportunity to get the world price for his grain, whether it be through the Winnipeg grain exchange or through some other agency established to handle grain.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: As the hon. member knows, rye has been on the grain exchange and traded in for some time. It has fluctuated widely. Does the hon. member think it would be a good thing to have wheat fluctuate like that because, after all, that would be very important to the income of the farmer and important to the consumer of bread?

The hon. member for Rosthern knows the reason rye did an apache dance, if I can call it that, was that there was nothing else to play with. Wheat would never do the same thing because there is plenty of wheat. Certainly the gamblers were in the rye market because they had been shut out from many others. I hear a lot of raucous laughter over here. Does someone else want to take a crack at it?

The hon. gentleman has stated that the farmer may sell his grain in the form of auctions. I think that is a legitimate field. I think it is also legitimate for the miller to be able to buy an option so that he will know what his flour will cost him when he is ready to deliver it. Those are two legitimate transactions on the exchange. But does the hon. member think the other people who come in and buy and sell grain ten or twenty or thirty times over on the exchange are engaged in legitimate transactions?

No, I do not think so. The question is a very fair one. But what the hon. member is suggesting would be utterly impossible, I say with great respect, to carry out in any grain trading at all, because when a man comes on the exchange he cannot carry 1,000 bushels on his back, and under the system my hon. friend advocates
he would need to have the actual grain or to prove he had had it. I think that would be quite unworkable. When my hon. friend asks, do I believe in a man taking a chance? I would say that if he wants to gamble I do not see anything wrong with it.
The hon. member sees no harm in that?

May I go a step farther and show the hon. member just what the position is. Let us say that you deal with somebody on the grain exchange and you have no grain. You have advertised the fact that you have no grain. The company that takes your bid and makes your purchase for you thinks you owe it a good deal of money, but I have had several lawsuits of this kind and I know how they came out. All the purchaser has to do is to go into court and say that it was a gambling transaction, that he had no grain to deliver and never expected any, and that lets him out. The James Richardson Company is a case in point which went to the court of appeal in Manitoba. The courts will not enforce such a contract because they say it is a gaming contract. I know there are people who gamble on the exchange in Winnipeg, Chicago, Toronto, Montreal, New York, London, Berlin, Rotterdam and every other place I know of. I saw a ten-cent pinochle game in the lobby just now.
That is not gambling with the necessities of life.

I think I have answered the hon. member in my humble way as best I know how, but if there are any more in the class who want to be bright this evening I am still here and am available for such questions as they may ask. With that I am going to close.
I know there are evils in the Winnipeg grain exchange. I think the hon. member was close to touching on one of them just a moment ago. But let us be fair about these matters. Why should we take away from an individual the right to use his judgment as to what his grain is -worth? Remember this, that these people are not in the exporting business. All our grain exporting from this country, certainly up to not many years ago, was handled by New York houses. The Dreyfus company was, I think, the biggest one, if my memory serves me correctly. The elevator company with which you do business is not gambling with your wheat and is not gambling on the Winnipeg grain exchange. It gets its living from a service which it gives in the way of handling charges, insurance, storage and that
48S
Agricultural Products Act

sort of thing. So just because somebody is able to build a big house in Assiniboine park, Winnipeg-and some of these fellows did build big houses there, and they are all trying to sell them now-that is no argument for closing the exchange. I know it is said: Look at these fellows who came up here from Minneapolis and are living in these big houses. But some of them are tearing them down now to avoid paying taxes.
They should take them over for C.C.F. headquarters.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Before the hon. member closes, will he answer one more question? If there is an apparent over-supply of wheat in the world or an under-demand as happened in 1932, does he not think the people who are trying to make money on the exchange when there is an over-supply or an under-demand, help to drive the price of wheat down lower than it otherwise would go?
Surely the hon. member must know that when they sell that grain they have to buy it back.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Yes, but if they sell it high and drive it down several cents they can buy it back at a lower price.
That is theoretical. If the price goes up three cents, they have made a loss.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It did not happen in 1932.
I do not know whether it did or not. I am prepared to accept the hon. member's word. But that is one of those things that will happen. Nothing has ever been airtight in any business yet.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Does the hon. member not think-

Give me just a minute of my time to finish my speech. That is not a very reasonable request, I know, but I would like time to conclude, even though it be a matter of grace from my hon. friend the member for Rosthern.
I have taken this position for two reasons. One is that I represent a large farming area and I do not want any doubt in their minds where I stand. I know that what I am saying will be quite unpopular there. But I so believe in what I am saying, in the freedom of the individual to dispose of his property as he sees fit, that by the time some people over there have made up their minds who will be the next leader when the general election comes, my constituents will have gained in intelligence and will have had an excellent
lesson like my hon. friends to my immediate left, and by that time they will all agree with me.
On motion of Mr. Herridge the debate was adjourned.

Mr. ST. LAURENT: It is intended tomorrow to continue with this debate and afterwards take up resolution No. 6 on today's order paper, to introduce a measure to assist in meeting the increased cost of production of gold produced from gold mines during the three years commencing on December 1, 1947. If that resolution is adopted the minister might, with the unanimous consent of the house, introduce a bill and have it read the first time so that it could be distributed and the members have an opportunity of studying it during the recess. After that, if there were time, we would proceed with the resolution under government notices of motion dealing with the tariff items in schedule V to the general agreement on tariffs and trade.

Is it the intention to sit tomorrow evening?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It is the intention to sit until the usual hour of adjournment unless we should exhaust the business on the order paper before that, which, while desirable, may not. be probable.

Will the minister give consideration to not sitting tomorrow evening? Many members want to catch trains tomorrow night and adjourning at six would give them an opportunity to do so.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I should not like to undertake to say that the house would adjourn at six o'clock, because it would be the desire of most hon. members that this resolution be disposed of. It has to be disposed of, and I think hon. members would also wish to have before them the terms of the bill which it is the intention of the government to introduce dealing with assistance to the gold mines. If these could be disposed of before six o'clock I am sure it would be the desire of all to meet the wishes of such hon. members as wish to leave early.

Would the minister consider sitting through the dinner recess from six o'clock to eight o'clock?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: We shall endeavour tomorrow to meet the convenience of hon. members in that regard and not interfere with the plans they have made for the trains leaving Ottawa in the evening.
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Friday, December 19, 1947
